blog_posts.title: Fall Home Staging Ideas: A Room-by-Room Guide
blog_posts.text:
Fall home staging works best when warmth sits on top of a clean, neutral base. Wool throws, wood, greenery and a few harvest accents in the entry, living room and dining room help buyers picture cooler months in the space. Clear counters and strong lighting keep rooms reading spacious in listing photos. Fall 2026 interiors favor tactile natural materials, earthy color and collected pieces, and those ideas translate into staging that photographs well and packs away fast.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Warmth plus restraint wins. Layer texture over a neutral base and cap seasonal accents at about three per gathering room.
Inventory across 46 US metros was up 4.7% year over year in July 2026 and homes averaged 45 days on market, so listings compete for attention longer.
Fall 2026 palettes center on moss green and chocolate brown with burgundy and plum accents. Burnt orange and mustard belong in textiles.
Harvest styling appeals broadly. Halloween and holiday-specific decor narrows the buyer pool.
Daylight saving time ends November 1, so evening showings run dark. Lighting matters as much as decor.
Run the furnace, service the fireplace and clear the gutters before the first showing. Fall buyers notice mechanicals.
Fall Listings Are Competing With More Inventory

Sellers listing this fall are sharing the market with more homes than they were a year ago. The July 2026 REMAX National Housing Report, which surveys 46 US metro areas, found the number of homes for sale rose 4.7% year over year and 2.8% from June. Months’ supply of inventory reached 3.0, up from 2.7 in June and 2.9 a year earlier.

Homes also took slightly longer to go under contract. Days on market averaged 45 in July, three days longer than June and one day longer than July 2025. Season is one of several factors that shape how long it takes to sell a house, along with condition, pricing and local demand. The median sales price held flat at $450,000 month over month and was 3.4% higher year over year, and the close-to-list price ratio stayed at 99%.

Conditions vary sharply by metro. Miami posted an 11.8% year-over-year increase in closed transactions in July while months’ supply there sat at 6.2, and Hartford averaged 18 days on market with months’ supply of 0.9. Local numbers matter more than national averages. What holds across markets is that presentation is one of the few variables a seller controls outright, and more competing listings means each set of photos has to earn a click.

THE FALL 2026 PALETTE

Two grounding neutrals, two deep accents and two warm textile tones.

FOUR DIRECTIONS FOR SELLERS

01

Tactile natural materials

Wool, stone, wood and woven textures lead the fall season, along with rising interest in sculptural stone pieces.

02

An earthy palette with accents

Moss green and chocolate brown anchor the season, with burgundy and plum as accents.

03

Organic modern

Clean lines paired with raw, natural textures. This style photographs well because it reads calm without feeling empty.

04

Collected and vintage pieces

One-of-a-kind finds, handmade ceramics and artisan accents add personality without clutter. Woven baskets and trays add color, pattern and texture at once.

Room by Room: Where Seasonal Layers Belong
Entry and Front Door

Curb appeal drives the first listing photo and the first ten seconds of a showing. The fundamentals that apply in warmer months still hold, with a seasonal adjustment. Rake leaves off the lawn and walkways, clear gutters of visible debris and replace tired summer planters with mums in warm tones. A harvest wreath built from dried citrus, pinecones and berries reads seasonal without committing to a holiday. If the front door already carries color, such as a deep red or navy, let the door stay the focal point and keep everything around it quiet.

Inside the door, build for weather. Fall showings bring rain and mud in most of the country and early snow in northern markets. A heavy-duty mat, a boot tray and a few hooks keep the entry from collapsing into a pile of wet coats and show buyers the space functions year round.

Living Room

Texture carries the living room in fall. Drape one chunky knit throw over a sofa arm and fold a second in a contrasting tone across a chair or bench. Add two or three pillows in wool, velvet or boucle. If the home has a fireplace, clear the mantel to three objects at most and angle seating toward it so the feature reads as the reason the room is arranged the way it is. One large piece of abstract art in warm neutrals can tie the palette together. A woven basket beside the sofa gives remotes and chargers somewhere to disappear before a showing.

Kitchen

Buyers are measuring workspace, so counters stay mostly bare. One styled moment is plenty: a wooden board holding apples or pears, or a small tray with cinnamon sticks, star anise and dried orange slices. Both add color and texture, and both double as a low-key scent source that does not require a candle.

Dining Room

Buyers touring in fall are often running the math on hosting. Thanksgiving falls on November 26 this year, and a simple table setting helps a buyer picture the room in use. A runner, a low centerpiece and two candlesticks do the job. Burgundy twisted tapers sit right inside the 2026 palette. Skip full place settings at every chair, which crowd the table and hide its size. A ceramic pitcher with rose hips or dried branches works well on a console or sideboard.

Primary Bedroom

Swap lightweight summer bedding for a heavier duvet in a warm neutral and lay a wool or knit blanket across the foot of the bed. Strip nightstands to a lamp and one small object each. The target is a room that reads restful and ready for cold nights, not a room that reads decorated.

Bathrooms

Bathrooms take the smallest dose. A rust or chocolate hand towel, a folded stack of white towels and one small plant is the whole assignment. Clear the counter of everything personal, including toothbrushes and prescriptions, and check that grout and caulk look clean under the warmer bulbs going in elsewhere.

Stage the Systems, Not Just the Surfaces

Fall showings put a home’s mechanicals on display in a way summer showings do not. Buyers notice a cold room, a draft at the window and a fireplace that clearly has not been touched.

Run the furnace before the first showing and replace the filter. A system that has sat idle since spring often throws a burning-dust smell on startup, which is easy to clear in advance and hard to explain in the moment. Set the thermostat around 68 degrees for showings so buyers keep their coats off and stay longer.

Have a working fireplace inspected and swept, then stage it with neatly stacked wood. A gas fireplace should be lit or ready to light. Clean gutters, check that downspouts drain away from the foundation and reseal obvious gaps around doors and windows. Confirm smoke and carbon monoxide detectors work, since more buyers ask about them once heating season starts.

Lighting and Scent After the Time Change

Daylight saving time ends November 1, which pushes late-afternoon showings into darkness for the rest of the listing season. Turn on every lamp and overhead fixture before buyers arrive rather than lighting rooms as the tour moves through them. Use warm white bulbs in the 2700K range so rooms read inviting instead of clinical, and match color temperature across fixtures in the same room. Open blinds fully for daytime showings.

Flameless tapers and pillars give the same glow as real candles without leaving an open flame in a house full of strangers. Keep scent restrained. A pot of cinnamon, cloves and orange peel simmering before a showing reads as welcoming, while heavy sprays and strongly scented candles read as cover-up.

How Much Fall Decor Is Too Much

Seasonal styling should support the house, not audition against it. Roughly three seasonal touches in the main gathering rooms is a workable ceiling. Harvest themes such as gourds, wheat and warm textiles appeal to a wide range of buyers. Halloween and holiday-specific decor narrows that range fast.

Not every room needs a seasonal layer. A bathroom can carry a rust hand towel. A bedroom does not need a pumpkin on the dresser.

Price point shapes the dose too. Cozy seasonal styling suits starter and mid-priced homes well. Heavier fall themes tend to feel off in higher-end listings, where one arrangement at the entry plus quality textiles in the living spaces is usually the right amount.

Photo Timing, Halloween and the Holiday Stretch

Listing photos do most of the early selling, which makes timing worth planning. Photos loaded with pumpkins and orange throws look dated if the home is still active in December. A neutral base styled with warm textiles, wood and greenery carries from September through winter, and heavier seasonal accents can be added in person for showings instead of baked into the photos. Professional photography sits near the top of any home selling checklist for exactly this reason.

Halloween lands on a Saturday this year, which overlaps with prime weekend showing time. Sellers listing that week can keep pumpkins and skip anything with a face on it, since both are easy to move off the porch an hour before a tour. Sellers listing in October or November can ask their agent whether reshooting makes sense once the listing carries into the holidays.

Decor Sits on Top of the Basics

Seasonal styling only performs on a home that is already clean, decluttered and maintained. Deep cleaning, minor repairs and removing personal items come first, and these 10 expert tips for staging a home to sell cover which rooms to prioritize. Sellers weighing whether the effort pays off can read more on what home staging is and why it is worth it. Staging is positioning rather than remodeling, and the goal is to bring a home’s existing features forward.

With that foundation in place, the fall layers above help a listing hold attention in a season with more homes competing for it. For buyers who just closed, the same edit works as a straightforward seasonal refresh. A local REMAX agent can advise on how much seasonal styling fits the home, the price point and the neighborhood.

Frequently Asked Questions
Does fall home staging actually help a house sell?

Staging is designed to help buyers read a home’s best features quickly, both online and in person. In fall that means warm lighting, clear surfaces and texture that makes rooms feel comfortable in cooler weather. With inventory in the July 2026 REMAX National Housing Report up 4.7% year over year across 46 US metros, presentation is one lever a seller fully controls.

What should a seller stage first in the fall?

The entry and the living room. Curb appeal and the front door drive the first listing photo, and the living room is where texture does the most work. Clear leaves from walkways, add mums in warm tones, then layer knit throws and wool or velvet pillows indoors.

Should listing photos include fall decorations?

Keep photos on a neutral base of warm textiles, wood and greenery so they still work if the home is active in December. Heavier seasonal accents can be added in person for showings. A listing that carries into the holidays may warrant a conversation with the agent about reshooting.

How should sellers handle Halloween while a home is listed?

Halloween falls on a Saturday in 2026, which overlaps with weekend showings. Pumpkins, gourds and warm textiles read as harvest and appeal broadly. Skip costumes, faces, cobwebs and anything oriented toward a single holiday, and move porch decor aside before a tour.

What temperature should a house be set to for fall showings?

Around 68 degrees is a common setting. A comfortable house keeps buyers in their tour longer and out of their coats. Run the furnace and change the filter before the first showing so a system that sat idle all summer does not throw a burning-dust smell mid-tour.

blog_posts.title: How Much Does Putting 20% Down Really Save You?
blog_posts.text:
Putting 20% down reduces the amount you need to borrow and in most cases removes private mortgage insurance (PMI) from a conventional mortgage. That lowers both the monthly housing cost and the interest paid over the life of the loan. The actual savings depend on the home price, interest rate, loan term and the smaller down payment being compared. A 20% down payment can cut financing costs, but it should still leave enough cash for closing costs, moving expenses, repairs and other financial priorities.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
You do not need 20% down for many mortgage programs.
A 20% down payment reduces the loan balance and generally avoids PMI on a conventional loan.
On a $350,000 home, 20% down is $70,000 and leaves a $280,000 loan.
FHA mortgage insurance follows different rules than conventional PMI.
Property taxes, homeowners insurance and HOA dues do not change with a larger down payment.
What Does 20% Down Actually Do?

With a 20% down payment, the buyer finances the remaining 80% before any costs or fees that may be added to the loan. For conventional financing, 20% is an important threshold because PMI is generally not required at that level. PMI protects the lender rather than the borrower, so removing it lowers the monthly cost of the mortgage without changing anything about the coverage the buyer carries. For a closer look at how that cost works, see what PMI is and how to avoid it.

How Would a Bigger Down Payment Be Beneficial to Borrowers?

A bigger down payment reduces the starting mortgage balance. If the interest rate and loan term stay the same, borrowing less lowers the required principal-and-interest payment and reduces the total interest paid over the life of the loan. A larger down payment also gives the buyer more equity from the start.

Lower Loan Balance

Every additional dollar paid upfront is one less dollar that needs to be borrowed. That difference compounds across a 30-year term, which is why the same home can carry two very different total costs depending on the down payment. Program minimums vary widely, from no money down on some government-backed loans to 3% on some conventional programs, so the starting point is not the same for every buyer. A breakdown by loan type is available in how much a down payment on a house is.

Potentially Lower Monthly Housing Cost

On a conventional loan, reaching 20% down can also remove PMI from the initial payment. Property taxes, homeowners insurance and HOA fees are separate and do not disappear with a larger down payment. When comparing options, look at the full monthly cost of homeownership rather than the mortgage balance alone.

What 20% Down Looks Like on a $350,000 Home

Cash down and the loan balance that follows, before any costs or fees added to the loan.

20% DOWN PAYMENT


$70,000


Loan amount: $280,000
DOWN PAYMENT	CASH DOWN	LOAN AMOUNT
5%	$17,500	$332,500
10%	$35,000	$315,000
15%	$52,500	$297,500
20%	$70,000	$280,000

Figures exclude closing costs, prepaid taxes and insurance, moving expenses, repairs, and cash a buyer may want to hold in reserve.

How Much Could 20% Down Save on the Monthly Payment?

There is no single dollar amount because the savings depend on the rate, term and smaller down payment being compared. On the same $350,000 home, 10% down leaves a $315,000 mortgage, while 20% down leaves a $280,000 mortgage. That is $35,000 less to finance.

At the same interest rate and loan term, financing $35,000 less lowers principal and interest. A conventional buyer putting 20% down would also avoid PMI, while a buyer putting 10% down may need it. Because PMI pricing varies by credit profile, loan-to-value ratio and insurer, an actual lender quote gives a more useful comparison than a generic estimate. Buyers who are still setting a price range can also compare how much home they can afford at several down payment levels.

How the Savings Shift With Rate and Term

The gap between a 10% and a 20% down payment is not a fixed dollar amount. It moves with the interest rate and the length of the loan.

At a higher interest rate, the same $35,000 difference in loan size carries a larger monthly cost, so the payment gap between the two options widens. At a lower rate, that gap narrows. A comparison run several months ago may no longer describe what the same two options look like now.

Loan term works the same way. A 30-year term spreads the balance across more payments, which lowers the monthly amount but raises the total interest paid. A 15-year term does the opposite. A buyer weighing 20% down against a shorter term is often comparing two different routes to the same goal of paying less interest, and a lender can price both side by side.

Mortgage insurance adds a third variable. PMI is priced on the credit profile, the loan-to-value ratio and the insurer, so two buyers putting 10% down on the same home can carry different PMI costs. That is the piece a generic online calculator is least likely to get right.

What 20% Down Does Not Change

A larger down payment reduces the loan amount, but several costs stay where they are. Property taxes, homeowners insurance, HOA dues and utilities are tied to the property rather than to the loan balance. Closing costs are calculated on the purchase price and the loan, so paying more upfront does not erase them.

Credit score, debt-to-income ratio and loan program also continue to influence the interest rate a lender offers. A 20% down payment can strengthen an application, but it does not replace the rest of the underwriting picture. Two buyers putting the same amount down on the same home can receive different rates. Comparing offers means looking at the rate, the mortgage insurance, the lender charges and the cash required at closing together rather than one line at a time.

Should I Put 20% Down on a House?

Putting 20% down on a mortgage may make sense if it reduces borrowing costs without leaving the buyer short of cash. It lowers the mortgage balance, reduces principal and interest, and generally eliminates PMI on a conventional loan. A buyer may prefer a smaller down payment if using that much cash would leave too little for closing costs, repairs, moving or an emergency reserve. The full set of tradeoffs is covered in the pros and cons of putting 20 percent down.

Compare the Full Loan Cost

Ask lenders for loan estimates for the down payment levels and mortgage programs under consideration. Compare the interest rate, principal and interest, mortgage insurance, lender charges, cash to close, and other costs. A mortgage preapproval can help define the loan amount and financing options available before an offer goes in.

Keep Enough Cash After Closing

A larger down payment can reduce financing costs, but keeping cash available after closing matters just as much. Repairs, maintenance, moving expenses and unexpected costs can arise within the first months of ownership. Planning for the first year of homeownership helps determine how much of a savings balance to commit to the down payment.

FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS
Do you need to put 20% down on a house?

No. Down payments vary by loan program, home price, available savings and the buyer’s circumstances. The 20% figure matters because it is the point where PMI is generally not required on a conventional mortgage, not because it is a minimum.

Can you put less than 20% down on a house?

Yes. Many buyers purchase with less than 20% down. A smaller down payment creates a larger mortgage balance and may add mortgage insurance or other loan costs, depending on the program.

Does a conventional loan require 20% down?

No. Some conforming conventional programs allow eligible borrowers to put as little as 3% down. The 20% figure is commonly associated with avoiding PMI, not with a universal minimum down payment.

Can you put 20% down on an FHA loan?

Yes. An eligible borrower can put 20% down on an FHA loan. FHA mortgage insurance follows different rules from conventional PMI, so a 20% FHA down payment does not automatically remove mortgage insurance.

Can I avoid PMI without putting 20% down?

Some loan structures and lender programs handle mortgage insurance differently, and pricing varies. A full breakdown is available in the guide to avoiding PMI.

Can PMI be removed later?

Often, yes. Conventional borrowers may be able to request cancellation once the loan reaches applicable thresholds, and automatic termination rules can also apply. FHA and VA loans follow different rules.

blog_posts.title: Coffee Table Decor Ideas for Staging a Home to Sell
blog_posts.text:
The coffee table is one of the first surfaces a buyer notices when walking into a living room during a showing. It can also be the perfect way to market your home with a picturesque coffee table listing shot.

Deciding what goes on a coffee table is one of the cheapest staging moves available to a seller. It doesn’t take much time, it could cost practically nothing, and it changes how a room photographs.

Why the coffee table matters when selling a home

Staging works by helping buyers picture their own life in the space instead of yours. The Real Estate Staging Association reports that staged homes spend 73 per cent less time on the market than homes that were not staged. The living room does a lot of that work, because it is where buyers stop, look around and form an opinion about how the home lives.

A cluttered table reads as a storage problem. A bare table reads as an empty rental. A table with three or four considered objects reads as a home somebody takes care of. That is the target.

For the full room-by-room version of this work, the REMAX home staging guide covers the rest of the house.

Nine coffee table decor ideas that work in listing photos

The goal of a stylistic coffee table is one that looks composed and intentional. Don’t just leave your table cluttered, as is. Think about how books, lighting, or art can help shape the table while complementing the rest of the living room.

Pottery accents

Ceramic vases and vessels add height without adding too much visual noise. Two pieces of different heights may work better than a matched pair. Keep them empty or add a plant. Skip anything with a strong glaze color that fights the room. Neutral colors and patterns are the way to go.

Florals and greenery

Live greenery signals upkeep. Buyers may read that as a well-maintained home. A small trailing plant or a group of succulents can photograph better than a overwhelming bouquet of flowers. Fresh flowers need replacing every few days during an active listing, so a hardy plant is the lower-maintenance option.

Aesthetic coasters

Coasters are the rare staging item that can be used for both decor and function. A stone or marble set stacked in a corner of the table fills space at low height and hints that the surface is usable. They also protect the table during showings which is very important.

Chess board

A game board suggests the room gets used for something other than screen time. It works best on a large table with room to spare on either side. On a small table it can take over. Set the pieces mid-game rather than in starting rows for a lived-in look.

Decorative tray

The tray is the one of the most useful object on this list. It draws a border around the display. It also keeps small items from drifting. It can give the whole arrangement one clean edge in photos as well. A tray makes cleanup fast, since the entire setup lifts off in one motion before a showing.

Coffee table books

A stack of two or three hardcovers adds height and a horizontal line that balances taller objects. Choose broad subjects such as architecture, travel, design or photography. Books tied to politics, religion or a specific fandom pull attention toward the current owner. That’s the opposite of what staging is for.

Vintage glass

Cut glass and colored glass catch light. This can help a dim living room read brighter in photos and in person. One piece can be enough depending on the size of your table. A bowl can hold something simple such as citrus or matchbooks. It can also stay empty as a sculptural object and art piece.

Tapered candles

Candles add vertical lines to a mostly horizontal surface. Grouped in odd numbers at staggered heights, they are one of the easiest ways to make a flat table look composed. Leave them unlit during showings. An open flame is a liability with strangers moving through the house. Scent can also be a gamble with buyers who have allergies or sensitivities.

Sculptures

A sculptural object is the piece that makes a table look styled rather than tidied. Bust reproductions, abstract forms and carved wood shapes all do the same job. Keep the scale under control. Anything that blocks the sightline across the room works against the photo.

How to build the display in five steps
Clear the table completely. Every remote, coaster, charger and magazine comes off before anything goes back on.
Anchor with a tray. Place it off-centre rather than dead middle. It gives the eye a starting point.
Group in odd numbers and vary the height. Three objects at three different heights is the standard formula. A tall vase, a medium stack of books, a low bowl.
Leave roughly two thirds of the surface open. Empty space is what separates a staged table from a decorated one. Buyers need to see the table, not just what is on it.
Check it through a camera. Photograph the table from standing height and from the doorway. Objects that look balanced in person often crowd each other in a photo.
What to leave off the coffee table
Remotes, chargers and visible cords
Mail, paperwork and bills
Family photos, diplomas and anything with a name on it
Medication, vitamins and personal care items
Valuables and anything fragile enough to worry about during an open house
Toys, pet items and chew marks in the sightline
Strong scents from diffusers or plug-ins, which buyers often read as covering something up

Depersonalizing is the part sellers tend to resist. It is also the part that most reliably helps a buyer imagine their own belongings in the room. More of that thinking is covered in these 10 expert tips for staging your home to sell.

What size coffee table works best for staging?

Before anything goes on the table, the table itself has to fit the room. A piece that is too large eats the walkway and makes the living room photograph smaller than it is. A piece that is too small disappears between the sofa and the rug. The general target is a table about two thirds the length of the sofa, sitting at roughly sofa-seat height.

Sellers do not need to buy anything. If the current table is oversized, blocking traffic or damaged enough to distract, borrowing a smaller piece from elsewhere in the house or removing it entirely is usually the better call. An empty floor reads cleaner than a crowded one.

Proportion is where most coffee table displays go wrong. A few working rules:

Decor should sit below the eye level of someone seated on the sofa, so conversation is not blocked
The tallest object should measure roughly two thirds the height of the sofa back or less
Keep about 18 inches of clearance between the table and surrounding furniture so walkways stay open.
A large rectangular table can carry two small groupings. A small round table should carry one

Clear walkways matter as much as the decor itself. Buyers who have to sidestep furniture register the room as smaller than it is.

Recently bought? The same rules apply as a refresh

Not everyone reading this is selling. A coffee table refresh is one of the fastest ways for a recent buyer to make a new living room feel settled, especially in the stretch after moving day when most of the house is still in boxes. One styled surface gives the eye somewhere to land while the rest of the room catches up.

The difference is that a new owner gets to put the personality back in. The framed photo, the souvenir from a trip, the stack of books nobody else would pick. Staging strips those out on purpose. Living in a home is when they go back on the table.

Keeping the table showing-ready

An active listing means the table needs to reset in under a minute. A few habits make that realistic:

Keep a basket or bin nearby for remotes, mail and anything that lands on the table during the day
Photograph the finished display and keep the photo on your phone as a reference for resetting it
Wipe the surface before every showing, since stone and glass tops show dust and fingerprints in photos
Replace or remove greenery the moment it starts to look tired

Whether staging pays off depends on the property and the local market, and a local agent is the right person to judge that. A REMAX agent can walk the home, flag the rooms worth the effort and point out the ones already working. Find out whether staged homes sell faster, then connect with a REMAX agent in your area to build a prep plan for your listing.

Frequently asked questions
What should go on a coffee table when staging a home?

Three to five items in varied heights, usually a tray, a stack of books, something living such as a plant, and one sculptural object. Leave most of the surface open and remove anything personal, including photos, mail and medication.

How many items should be on a coffee table?

Three to five for most tables. Groupings in odd numbers tend to look more natural than pairs. A small round table can look crowded with more than three objects, while a large rectangular table can carry two separate groupings.

Should coffee table books be stacked or fanned out?

Stacked. Two or three hardcovers in a neat pile add height and a clean horizontal line. Fanning books across the surface eats space and reads as clutter in photos. A small object placed on top of the stack gives the grouping a finished look.

Should candles be lit during a showing?

No. Unlit candles still add height and shape to a display without the fire risk of open flame in a house full of strangers. Strong scents also create problems for buyers with allergies or sensitivities.

Can you stage a coffee table without buying anything?

Usually, yes. Most homes already have books, a bowl, a tray or a plant somewhere else in the house. Staging a coffee table is more often about editing and rearranging what is already there than about buying new decor.

Does coffee table decor affect how a home sells?

On its own, no single surface sells a house. What sits on the coffee table contributes to the larger impression a living room makes in photos and showings, and the living room is one of the rooms buyers weigh most heavily. Ask a local agent how much staging effort makes sense for your property and market.

blog_posts.title: Buying a Home in August 2026 as a First-Time Buyer
blog_posts.text:
Buying a home in August 2026 means shopping a market with more listings than a year ago and a median price that was unchanged from the month before. The July 2026 REMAX National Housing Report, the most recent release available during August, recorded a median sales price of $450,000 across 46 metro areas. That figure was flat compared to June 2026 and 3.4% higher than July 2025.

Inventory was up 4.7% year over year. Months’ supply of inventory measured 3.0, compared to 2.7 in June and 2.9 a year earlier. More listings did not arrive with a lower entry price. For buyers purchasing a first home, the distance between more options and more affordable options is where the reported data gets difficult.

The national snapshot behind buying a home in August 2026

These are the headline figures from the July 2026 REMAX National Housing Report, based on MLS data across 46 metro areas.

NATIONAL SNAPSHOT: JULY 2026

Closed transactions	Not reported as a total	▼ Down 5.7%	▲ Up 2.5%
New listings	Not reported as a total	▼ Down 2.7%	▲ Up 1.4%
Inventory	Not reported as a total	▲ Up 2.8%	▲ Up 4.7%
Months' supply of inventory	3.0	Up from 2.7	Up from 2.9

Close-to-list price ratio	99%	Unchanged	Unchanged

Where first-time buyers faced the tightest conditions
The reported entry price was higher than a year earlier

A median sales price of $450,000, up 3.4% year over year, works out to roughly $14,800 more than the same month in 2025. Buyers who spent the previous 12 months saving toward a target figure were measuring against a higher one by July.

Some metros reported homes closing above list price

The 99% national close-to-list price ratio indicates that, on average across the 46 metros, homes closed just under asking price. Individual markets differed. Hartford, CT reported a 105% close-to-list ratio alongside 0.9 months’ supply and an average of 18 days on market, the lowest figures for both metrics in the report. San Francisco, CA also reported 105%. New York, NY reported 102%. Chicago, Philadelphia, Providence, Richmond, St. Louis and Trenton each reported 101%.

Lower-priced metros often reported tighter supply

The spread between metros was wide. San Francisco, CA reported a $1,180,000 median sales price. Wichita, KS reported $250,000, the lowest in the report.

Several of the lowest-priced metros also reported some of the lowest months’ supply figures:

The metros reporting the largest year-over-year inventory gains carried higher medians: San Diego, CA up 48.1%, Los Angeles, CA up 45.5% and San Francisco, CA up 39.0%. Detroit, MI was an exception, reporting inventory up 43.0% against a $313,000 median.

Listings took longer to go under contract

Homes sold in July 2026 spent an average of 45 days on market, three days longer than in June 2026 and one day longer than July 2025. Individual metros ranged widely. San Antonio, TX reported 85 days on market with 6.0 months’ supply and a 97% close-to-list ratio. Miami, FL reported 77 days with 6.2 months’ supply and a 94% close-to-list ratio, the lowest ratio in the report. Phoenix, AZ reported 74 days and Tampa, FL reported 71.

Closing above asking was not the national average. The close-to-list price ratio measured 99%, unchanged from June 2026 and July 2025.
Supply measured higher. Months’ supply of inventory reached 3.0, up from 2.7 in June 2026.
How to read your local market before you shop

National averages describe 46 metro areas combined, not any single neighborhood. The REMAX National Housing Report tracks four metrics that describe local conditions.

Months’ supply of inventory. Total homes listed at month end divided by contracts signed during the month. In July 2026, this ranged from 0.9 in Hartford, CT to 6.2 in Miami, FL.
Days on market. The average number of days from listing until a property goes under contract. July 2026 ranged from 18 days in Hartford, CT to 85 days in San Antonio, TX.
Close-to-list price ratio. Sales price divided by list price. Above 100% means homes closed above asking price. Below 100% means below asking price. Miami’s 94% was the lowest in the report.
Year-over-year inventory change. A rising figure indicates more listings than the same month last year. A falling figure indicates fewer.

blog_posts.title: Turning Interest Into Offers: Amenities That Matter
blog_posts.text:
Certain home features do more than look good in listing photos. They shape how buyers feel walking through a space and how quickly interest turns into a written offer. The four amenities below consistently draw attention during showings and support a home’s perceived value at resale.

Key Takeaways
A well-designed walk-in closet adds organized storage and a sense of luxury to the primary suite.
A spa-inspired ensuite uses soft lighting and quality materials to create a calm retreat.
An open concept kitchen connects cooking, dining and gathering, a layout buyers rank among the most in-demand.
Functional outdoor living space extends usable square footage and appeals to buyers who want indoor-outdoor flow.
Why Do Amenities Influence Offers?

Buyers form fast impressions. Within the first few rooms, most have a sense of whether a home feels cared for and whether it fits how they want to live. Amenities that speak to comfort, storage and daily function give those impressions something concrete to hold onto.

A feature that solves a real problem, like where to store clothes or how to host a crowd, tends to stick in a buyer’s memory after the showing ends. That memory is often what separates a home that gets a second look from one that gets an offer. The four amenities below share a common thread. Each one improves how a home lives day to day, and each one is easy for buyers to picture themselves using.

What Makes a Walk-in Closet Worth the Investment?

A well-designed walk-in closet gives the primary suite organized storage and easy access to everyday items. The strongest versions use a mix of built-in shelving, drawers, hanging sections at two heights and a dedicated spot for shoes and accessories. A window or good overhead lighting keeps the space usable at any hour, and a center island or bench adds function without crowding the room.

Buyers often read a dedicated closet as a sign that the rest of the home was planned with the same care. During a showing, a closet that stays neat and shows off its storage tends to hold attention longer than one packed to the shelves. Sellers who edit their wardrobe down before listing let the space read as roomy, which supports the perceived value of the suite.

Why Do Buyers Respond to a Spa-inspired Ensuite?

A spa-inspired ensuite turns the primary bathroom into a retreat. The look leans on a few consistent elements: soft layered lighting, natural stone or large-format tile, a soaking tub or an oversized walk-in shower and warm textiles within reach. A separate water closet, dual vanities and a bench in the shower add the kind of function buyers notice. Muted colors and clean lines keep the room feeling calm rather than busy.

The goal is comfort that reads at a glance, not a full renovation. Even modest updates like a rainfall showerhead, fresh grout, new hardware and folded towels on open shelving can move a dated bathroom toward that spa feel. During a showing, an ensuite that feels serene gives buyers a reason to linger, and that pause often carries into how they judge the rest of the home.

What Makes an Open Concept Kitchen a Resale Priority?

An open concept kitchen connects cooking, dining and gathering in one continuous space. The layout keeps the cook part of the conversation instead of closed off behind a wall, and it lets light move through the main floor. A center island does the heavy lifting here. It offers prep space, casual seating and a natural gathering point for guests and family. Durable counters, ample storage and a clear sightline to the living area round out the appeal.

The layout suits both entertaining and daily routines, which is part of why flow and openness stay among the features buyers look for. Homes with a genuinely open plan tend to photograph well and show well, since the eye travels across the whole space at once. For sellers, keeping counters clear and defining each zone with a rug or lighting helps buyers picture how they would use the room.

How Does Outdoor Living Space Add Value?

Functional outdoor living space extends a home’s usable square footage beyond the walls. The strongest versions feel like an extension of the interior rather than a leftover patch of yard. A covered patio, an outdoor kitchen or grill station, defined dining and lounge zones and shade from a pergola or mature trees give buyers room to cook, host and relax outside.

A fireplace or fire feature stretches the usable season, and a pool or water element anchors the whole setup in warmer climates. Easy access from the main living area matters as much as the features themselves, since a smooth indoor-outdoor transition is what makes the space feel like part of the home. Buyers read this kind of setup as a lifestyle upgrade, and it gives listing photos a strong second act. For sellers, clean furniture groupings and a tidy planted look help the area read as living space rather than storage.

Which Amenities Matter Most for Your Home?

Small design choices add up when a home goes to market. Buyers respond to spaces that feel organized, calm and easy to live in, and the amenities above tend to do that work during a showing. Not every feature fits every property, and the right mix depends on price point, neighborhood and the type of buyer a home attracts.

A local REMAX agent can walk a seller through which upgrades carry the most weight for a specific home, which ones photograph well and where a small investment tends to show up in buyer interest.

A well-designed walk-in closet adds organized storage, easy access and a sense of luxury to the primary suite. Buyers often read a dedicated closet as a marker of a well-planned home, which supports the perceived value of the space.

What is a spa-inspired ensuite?

A spa-inspired ensuite is a primary bathroom designed as a calm retreat, with features like soft lighting, elegant materials and a soaking tub or oversized shower that create a relaxing setting.

Why are open concept kitchens popular with buyers?

Open concept kitchens connect cooking, dining and gathering in one space, which suits both entertaining and everyday family life. Flow and openness stay among the most in-demand features for resale.

Functional outdoor living space extends a home’s usable square footage and creates room for dining, lounging and entertaining. Buyers value strong indoor-outdoor flow as a lifestyle upgrade that adds to a property’s appeal.

blog_posts.title: Summer 2026 Home Trends: 4 Styles Shaping Homes Right Now
blog_posts.text:
Four trends define home design in summer 2026: seamless indoor-outdoor living, soft minimalism, Mediterranean revival and dedicated wellness spaces. They share more than a season. All four favor natural materials and warm neutrals, and all four rethink rooms around daily life instead of formality.

The wall between the kitchen and the patio is disappearing. Minimalism is getting warmer. Stone and terracotta are back. And the formal dining room is losing ground to the sauna. Here is what each trend looks like in real homes, and what it signals for buyers and sellers this season.

Key Takeaways
Seamless indoor-outdoor living treats the patio as a real room, with outdoor kitchens and shaded lounges furnished like interiors.
Soft minimalism warms up minimalist design with curved furniture and neutrals like sand, clay and sun-bleached stone.
Mediterranean revival builds on stone, terracotta and raw wood, with muted blues and olive greens on top.
Wellness spaces like saunas, meditation rooms and yoga terraces are replacing formal living and dining rooms.
Buyers consistently rank outdoor features among their most wanted home elements, and wellness-focused building has grown into a major global market.
What Is Seamless Indoor-Outdoor Living?

Seamless indoor-outdoor living erases the line between a home’s interior and its yard. Retractable glass walls open the living room straight onto the patio. The flooring keeps going, same material inside and out, so the transition disappears underfoot. The outdoor kitchen has grown up too. What used to be a grill on a slab is now a full entertaining space with prep counters and bar seating. And the shaded lounge nearby is furnished like an interior living room, down to the coffee table and the layered textiles.

Buyer demand backs this up. In the National Association of Home Builders’ What Home Buyers Really Want study, a patio was rated essential or desirable by 82% of buyers, among the highest marks of more than 200 features surveyed. A related industry survey found that 73% of residential design professionals favored covered outdoor rooms over a simple open yard. For sellers, a defined outdoor room can photograph like extra square footage. For buyers, it is worth asking how those structures were permitted before you write an offer. Our homebuyer’s hub covers what to check during due diligence.

What Is Soft Minimalism?

Soft minimalism keeps the restraint and drops the chill. The sharp angles and stark white walls are gone. In their place sit curved furniture, organic shapes and warm neutrals like sand, clay and sun-bleached stone. Texture does the work that color used to do. Think plaster and limewash walls, matte finishes, a boucle sofa, a nubby wool throw draped over the chaise. The room stays spare, but it finally feels lived in.

Picture a rounded sectional in oatmeal, a pair of walnut drum tables and one sculptural vase where a shelf of accessories used to be. That is the whole formula. For sellers, this is the most achievable trend to stage toward. A warm off-white on the walls, fewer but softer furniture pieces and some linen and wool will shift the entire feel of a room. No renovation required.

What Is Mediterranean Revival Style?

Mediterranean revival is the return of regional character. Stone, travertine, terracotta and raw wood form the base. Muted blues and olive greens sit on top of sun-faded neutrals. Walk into one of these rooms and you will notice the ceiling first, usually exposed wood beams, then the arched doorways and the hand-painted ceramics hung as wall art. The furniture is teak, simple and sturdy. This is not the heavy Tuscan look of the early 2000s.

Walls stay white or plaster-toned. Floors run to polished concrete or natural stone. Color comes from collected objects rather than saturated paint. The style reads most naturally in sun-drenched markets, but the materials travel well. Buyers touring homes this summer will spot terracotta tile and arched millwork in new construction and flips alike. Those materials also tend to age better than trend-driven synthetic finishes, which matters if you plan to hold the home for a while.

What Are Wellness Spaces in a Home?

Wellness spaces are rooms built for restoration, not for company. The formal living room is giving up its square footage to cold plunge and sauna combinations, meditation rooms, yoga terraces and sound-insulated quiet rooms. The entry point can be modest. A spare bedroom with a cork mat, a few floor cushions and good natural light does the job.

The market behind this shift is real. The Global Wellness Institute reported that the global wellness real estate market reached $876 billion in 2025, with the United States as the largest national market at $254 billion. The practical takeaway for homeowners is simple. Wellness features no longer read as niche. A sauna or a genuinely quiet room is now an amenity buyers can picture using the day they move in.

How Do Summer 2026 Home Trends Affect Buyers and Sellers?

For sellers, these trends amount to a staging roadmap. Warm neutrals. Edited furnishings. A defined outdoor seating area and one calm, uncluttered room. None of it requires structural work, and all of it matches what buyers are already seeing in design media.

For buyers, the trends work as a lens on cost. Retractable glass walls and outdoor kitchens are expensive to add later. Soft minimalist finishes and Mediterranean materials are mostly cosmetic. Knowing which is which helps you weigh one listing against another.

Frequently Asked Questions
What are the biggest home design trends for summer 2026?

The four defining trends are seamless indoor-outdoor living, soft minimalism, Mediterranean revival and dedicated wellness spaces. All four lean on natural materials and warm neutrals, and all four organize rooms around daily use rather than formality.

What is soft minimalism in interior design?

Soft minimalism keeps minimalist restraint but warms it up with curved furniture, organic forms and neutrals like sand, clay and sun-bleached stone. Texture leads through plaster, limewash and matte finishes, so spaces feel calm and livable rather than stark.

Do home design trends affect how a home sells?

Buyer preference research consistently shows that outdoor features like patios rank among the most wanted home elements, and staging choices influence how buyers perceive a listing. Trends do not replace fundamentals like price, condition and location, but aligning finishes and staging with current buyer taste can help a home show well.

How can sellers use summer 2026 trends without renovating?

Stick to cosmetic moves. Repaint in a warm off-white, pare furniture back to a few soft anchor pieces, add linen and wool for texture, set up a defined outdoor seating area and clear one room so it reads as a calm, flexible space. Each step aligns with the season’s trends at minimal cost.

blog_posts.title: Selling a Home With Mortgage Rates Near 7%
blog_posts.text:
Selling a Home With Mortgage Rates Near 7%

The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.76% as of September 10, 2026, according to Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey. That figure was 6.71% the week before and 6.35% a year earlier. Lender-quoted averages run higher than the survey. The Mortgage Bankers Association reported a 30-year fixed rate of 6.97% for the week ended September 11, 2026.

For a seller, the rate itself is not the problem. The problem is what the rate does to the buyer pool: how many people qualify, how much house they can carry and how much patience they bring to the negotiation. Selling in this environment is possible. It requires different decisions than the market of four years ago rewarded.

Buyers May Shop the Monthly Payment, Not the Price

A buyer with a $400,000 loan at 6.76% pays roughly $2,597 a month in principal and interest. The same loan at 6.00% runs about $2,398. That gap of nearly $200 a month is the entire reason a listing that would have drawn six offers in 2021 now draws one.

Rates can squeeze qualification from both directions. A higher rate raises the payment on any given loan amount, and lenders size the loan to the payment a borrower can document. The buyer looking at a home at the top of a price band this year is often the same household that looked at homes one band higher two years ago.

Three consequences could follow for the seller:

The pool of qualified buyers for any given asking price may be smaller than it was at lower rates.
The buyers who remain can be more sensitive to anything that adds cost after closing, including a roof near the end of its life or an aging furnace.
Offers may arrive with more conditions attached, since buyers have less cash left over after covering a larger payment.
What the Latest Housing Data Shows

Rates get the headlines but supply and time on market can be what changes a seller’s position. The July 2026 REMAX National Housing Report, covering 46 metro areas, found the number of homes for sale up 2.8% from June and 4.7% from July 2025. Months’ supply of inventory reached 3.0, up from 2.7 in June.

Homes also took longer to sell. Properties spent an average of 45 days on market in July, three days longer than in June and one day longer than July 2025. Closed transactions fell 5.7% from June while running 2.5% ahead of July 2025. New listings dipped 2.7% month over month and finished 1.4% above a year ago.

Prices did not crack. The median sales price was $450,000 in July, unchanged from June and 3.4% higher than July 2025. Buyers paid an average of 99% of asking price, which means homes that were priced correctly were still closing at or near the number on the listing.

That combination is the whole picture for a seller right now. Buyers have more options and more time to use them. Sellers who price to the market are still getting nearly full asking price. The gap between those two outcomes comes down to strategy rather than luck.

Pricing Strategy When Borrowing Costs Are High

Overpricing can cost sellers money. It costs more when buyers have more listings to compare and 45 days of typical marketing time to work with, because there are enough alternatives that a buyer simply skips the home rather than negotiating on it.

Practical guardrails:

Anchor to closed sales, not to active listings. Active listings show what other sellers hope to get. Closed sales show what buyers actually paid and what appraisers will support.
Price inside a search bracket, not just above one. Buyers filter in round numbers. A home listed at $455,000 misses every search capped at $450,000.
Treat the first two weeks as the real test. Showing traffic in the opening window can be the clearest read on whether the price matches the market. With homes averaging 45 days from listing to contract, a silent first two weeks is important information.
Set the reduction trigger before listing. Agreeing in advance on what happens if the home has no offers by a certain day removes the emotion from the decision later.
Watch the close-to-list ratio in the neighborhood. The national average sits at 99%. A local ratio well below that points to a price band where buyers are negotiating harder.
Concessions Often Move a Buyer Further Than a Price Cut

This is where high-rate markets behave differently. The same dollars spent on a rate buydown usually buy a bigger payment reduction than a price cut of equal size.

Take that $400,000 loan at 6.76%. Knocking $10,000 off the price lowers the loan to $390,000 and trims the payment by about $65 a month. Applying the same $10,000 to a permanent rate buydown could buy roughly half a percentage point, depending on the lender and the day’s point pricing. At 6.26%, the payment on the full $400,000 drops to about $2,465, a savings closer to $132 a month. Point pricing changes daily and varies by credit profile, so the actual trade should be run by a loan officer on the buyer’s specific file.

Common concession structures:

Permanent buydown. Seller-paid discount points lower the rate for the full loan term. Best suited to a buyer who plans to stay put.
Temporary buydown. A 2-1 structure cuts the rate by two points in year one and one point in year two before returning to the note rate. It lowers early payments without lowering the qualifying rate on most loan programs.
Closing cost credit. Applied to lender fees, title, prepaid taxes or insurance. Useful for a buyer who is tight on cash rather than tight on payment.
Repair credit. Money at closing in place of work the seller does not want to manage.

Concession caps vary by loan type and down payment, and credits cannot exceed actual costs. A lender confirms the limits before the terms go into the contract.

Condition and Presentation Carry More Weight Now

When a buyer stretches to make the payment, the repair list becomes a deal issue rather than a punch list. Items that used to get waived now get priced.

Handle the cheap fixes before listing: caulking, grout, sticking doors, burned-out bulbs, torn screens, running toilets.
Get documentation together for the expensive systems. Roof age, HVAC service records, water heater install date and any warranty paperwork answer questions before an inspector raises them.
Consider a pre-listing inspection. It converts surprises into disclosures, which are easier to price than discoveries made during the inspection period.
Invest in the photography. Most showings are decided on a phone screen before anyone drives over.
The Move on the Other Side of the Sale

Many sellers are also buyers, and the rate on the next loan is the real hesitation. Compare the payment on the next home against the equity coming out of the current one, the cost of staying put and the cost of any renovation that would make staying workable. Sellers who bought before 2022 often have enough equity to make a larger down payment on the next home, which offsets part of the higher rate.

What to Ask at the Listing Appointment
What have comparable homes actually closed at in the last 90 days, and how many days did each take?
How does this metro compare to the national averages for days on market and months’ supply?
How many recent transactions in this area included seller concessions, and at what size?
What is the plan if there are no offers after two weeks?
Is there new construction nearby, and what incentives are those builders advertising?

Local conditions vary widely. The REMAX National Housing Report tracks metros where months’ supply runs past five and others where it sits near one. A REMAX agent working the specific neighborhood can pull the numbers that determine the price.

blog_posts.title: How to Help Parents Downsize Their Home
blog_posts.text:
Helping parents downsize a longtime home is rarely just about moving boxes. The process can involve decades of belongings, familiar routines, family memories, and decisions about what comes next. Even when moving makes sense, leaving a longtime home can be difficult. The best approach is usually to involve your parents in the decisions, understand what the next home can accommodate, and divide the work into smaller steps. Helping doesn’t mean making every decision for your parents. Here are downsizing tips to help them navigate the move with greater confidence.

Key Takeaways
Start the conversation before the move becomes urgent.
Keep your parents involved in decisions about the home and their belongings.
Understand the next home’s space before sorting furniture and larger items.
Break the work into smaller projects instead of clearing the whole house at once.
Plan moving day around comfort, essential items, and a familiar setup in the new home.
Start With the Conversation

Before discussing boxes or listing the house, make sure everyone understands why downsizing their home is being considered.

Talk About What Has Become Difficult

Perhaps the yard is becoming difficult to maintain. Stairs may be inconvenient. A parent may want to live closer to family, or the home may simply have more space than they want to manage. Ask what your parent would like daily life to look like over the next few years. That conversation can help define what the next home needs to provide.

Avoid Turning the First Conversation Into a Deadline

If there is no urgent issue, you do not need to settle everything at once. Leaving a home after many years can take time to process.

Start by listening. Ask what has become difficult, what your parents want to keep, and where they might consider living. When parents remain involved in the decisions, the move is more likely to feel like their choice rather than something being arranged around them.

Choose the Next Home Before Making Too Many Decisions

It is much easier to decide what should move when you know where it is going.

Use the New Space as the Guide

A one-bedroom condo, smaller single-family home, senior community, or family member’s home will each have different space and storage limits.

Once you know the likely floor plan, measure the main rooms and larger pieces of furniture. Instead of asking, ‘What should we get rid of?’ ask, ‘What do you want in the new living room?’ That makes the decision more specific.

Think About Everyday Comfort

Consider stairs, entryways, bathroom access, laundry location, lighting, parking, storage, routine maintenance, and distance to family, or everyday services. The goal is not to predict every future need. It is to choose a home that works well now without creating obvious difficulties.

Organize the Home

Trying to clear and organize an entire home at once can quickly become overwhelming. Smaller projects make it easier to keep moving without turning every day into a major sorting session.

Start With Less Emotional Areas

Choose one room, closet, cabinet, or category at a time. Duplicate kitchen items, unused linens, old paperwork that can safely be discarded, or household items that have not been used in years can be easier places to begin. Photographs, letters, heirlooms, and family keepsakes can come later when there is more time to consider them carefully.

Keep the Sorting Categories Simple

A small ‘decide later’ group can prevent one difficult item from stopping an entire sorting session. Make sure those items are reviewed again before moving day.

Keep
Give to family
Donate
Sell
Discard
Decide later
Ask Family Members What They Actually Want

Parents sometimes keep furniture, dishes, collections, or other belongings because they expect children or grandchildren to want them someday. Ask rather than assume.

Give family members a reasonable deadline to choose items and arrange pickup. This can prevent unnecessary moving costs and reduce the chance of belongings being moved to the new home only to be sorted again later.

Handle Sentimental Items with Care

Some possessions matter because of the story attached to them rather than the object itself.

Preserve the Memory When the Item Cannot Come

If an item cannot reasonably move to the new home, consider photographing it. Old letters and photographs can sometimes be scanned, and family stories can be written down or recorded.

Be Careful with Important Records

For important documents, make sure you know which legal, financial, medical, tax, and property records need to be retained before anything is discarded. When there is uncertainty, check with the appropriate professional rather than guessing.

Plan the Move Before Moving Day

Moving day can be tiring and disruptive. A clear plan can reduce last-minute decisions and make the new home easier to settle into. Choose who will meet the movers, who will answer questions, and where your parent will be while the busiest work is happening. Clear roles can prevent several people from giving different instructions.

If possible, set up the bedroom, bathroom, and a familiar sitting area first. Recognizable furniture, photographs, and everyday items can make the new home feel more settled.

Know When Outside Help Would Make the Move Easier

Families do not have to manage every part of the move themselves. Depending on the situation, help may come from professional movers, organizers, estate-sale companies, junk-removal services, or specialists who work with older adults and their families. If health, legal, financial, or caregiving issues are involved, those questions should be handled by the appropriate professionals.

Frequently Asked Questions
How do I talk to my parents about downsizing?

Start by asking what they want and what has become difficult about the current home. Avoid presenting the move as a decision that has already been made for them unless circumstances require someone else to make those decisions.

Where should we start when downsizing my parents’ home?

Start by understanding the size and layout of the next home. Then work through one smaller, less emotional area at a time.

How long does it take to downsize a longtime home?

There is no standard timeline. A home with decades of belongings may take weeks or months to sort. Starting early reduces the pressure to make difficult decisions quickly.

Making the Move Easier for Everyone

Helping an aging parent downsize is as much about pace and respect as it is about moving. A well-planned transition gives your parent time to make decisions and helps the family focus on creating a comfortable next home.

A local REMAX agent can help your family understand the current home’s market, explore suitable housing options, and coordinate the real estate timeline while you manage the personal side of the move.

blog_posts.title: How to Sell a House with Solar Panels
blog_posts.text:
Selling a house with solar panels doesn’t have to complicate the transaction, but buyers will usually have more questions than they would for a typical home sale. Whether the system is owned, financed, leased, or covered by a power purchase agreement can affect the paperwork, financing, and closing process. Understanding those details before listing the property helps buyers evaluate the system with confidence and can prevent unnecessary delays later.

Key Takeaways
Confirm how the solar system is owned or financed.
Gather key solar documents before listing.
Leased or third-party systems may require transfer steps.
Solar can add appeal, but value varies by property.
Use factual claims instead of promising future savings.
What Do Solar Panels Mean for Home Value?

Solar panels may influence resale value, but the impact varies from one property to another. Factors such as the age and condition of the system, ownership structure, roof condition, local electricity costs, and buyer demand can all play a role. A local real estate agent can help compare recent sales, while a qualified appraiser determines the value when selling your house with solar panels.

Is the Solar System Owned, Financed, or Leased?

If the seller bought the solar system outright, ownership will generally convey with the property. A financed system may involve a remaining loan balance or other terms that need to be addressed. If the equipment is leased or covered by a power purchase agreement, a third party usually owns the system, and the contract may need to be transferred.

Third-party ownership can add extra steps to the sale, and the terms will depend on the specific agreement. Sellers should review the solar contract early to understand any transfer requirements, fees, or other obligations before listing the home. Understanding the connection between solar panels and selling your house starts with knowing who owns the system and whether any financing or lease terms still apply.

Contact the Solar Provider Before the Home Goes on the Market

Do not wait for an accepted offer to find out how a lease or other agreement is handled. Ask the provider what happens when the home is sold. Does the buyer need to qualify? Is there a transfer fee? Is a buyout available? Is there a remaining balance or recorded interest that the closing team needs to address?

Terms differ from one contract to another. Written instructions from the provider are far more useful than assuming your arrangement works like a friend’s or neighbor’s.

Put the Solar Records in One Place

A buyer may want to understand the system before deciding what it means for the home. Useful records can include:

Purchase, loan, or lease agreement
Installation date
System size
Equipment specifications
Warranties
Permits
Inspection or interconnection documents
Recent production information

Recent electric bills can also provide context, but they should be presented as historical records, not as a promise of what the next owner will pay. Electricity use, rates, weather, and system performance can all change.

Be Ready to Explain the Roof

Solar and roofing naturally raise questions together. Buyers may ask how old the roof is, whether it was replaced before the panels were installed, and what happens if roof work is needed later. If you have invoices or warranties for roof work, add them to the property file. If you do not know the cost or process for removing and reinstalling panels, avoid guessing. The solar installer or another qualified provider can give the buyer better information.

Help the Appraiser Understand the System

If the home is being appraised, make accurate system information easy to find. Ownership documents, equipment specifications, installation records and production history can help provide context. Because each appraisal is property-specific, the goal is to provide clear, reliable information about the solar system rather than suggest what it should be worth.

If the Panels Are Leased, Address the Transfer Early

Leased solar does not prevent a home sale, but it can add another party and another contract to the transaction. Depending on the agreement, the buyer may be able to assume the lease, the seller may have a buyout option, or another process may apply. The provider should explain the actual transfer requirements in writing. Share that information with your real estate and closing professionals early enough to avoid last-minute delays.

Market Solar with Facts, Not Promises

Solar can be an attractive feature, especially when buyers can quickly understand what they are acquiring. If the system is owned outright, say so. If warranties remain, identify them accurately. If production records are available, provide them.

Avoid statements such as “free electricity” or guaranteed future savings. A buyer’s future utility costs depend on factors the seller cannot control. Clear information tends to build more confidence than an aggressive claim.

What About Solar Tax Credits or Rebates?

If the solar system received a tax credit, rebate, or other incentive when it was installed, keep any related records with the property documents. Incentive programs and eligibility rules can vary by location and by the year the system was installed.

Sellers should avoid promising that a past tax credit or rebate will transfer to the buyer. If a buyer has questions about available incentives or tax treatment, they should confirm the details with a qualified tax professional or the program administrator.

Frequently Asked Questions
Is it hard to sell a house with solar panels?

Not necessarily. Owned systems may transfer relatively simply with the home. Leases, power purchase agreements, and some solar loans can require extra steps, which is why reviewing the agreement before listing is important.

Do solar panels increase resale value?

They may. Solar panels can add appeal for some buyers, but the effect on resale value varies by the system, ownership structure, property and local market.

What should you know about leasing solar panels when selling a house?

It depends on the solar agreement. A buyer may be able to assume the lease, the seller may have a buyout option, or other transfer terms may apply. Confirm the process directly with the solar provider before listing.

Preparing Your Solar Home for a Smooth Sale

When you are selling a home with solar panels, preparation matters more than salesmanship. Know who owns the system, understand any continuing obligations, and have the records ready before buyers begin asking questions.

A local REMAX agent can help you position the property, compare nearby sales, and keep the real estate side of the transaction moving. At the same time, the solar provider and other professionals handle system-specific requirements.

blog_posts.title: Should You Keep Your Current Home as a Rental When You Move?
blog_posts.text:
Moving to a new home doesn’t automatically mean selling the one you’re leaving behind. For some homeowners, keeping the property as a rental can create an additional income stream and the opportunity to continue building equity. But becoming a landlord also means taking on new financial responsibilities, legal obligations, and ongoing maintenance costs. Before deciding to rent out your current home, evaluate it as an investment property rather than simply the home you’ve lived in.

Key Takeaways
Compare realistic rent with the full cost of keeping the property.
Allow for vacancies, repairs, insurance, and management costs.
Check mortgage, insurance, HOA, and local rental requirements before converting the home.
Understand how rental income and a later sale may affect your taxes.
Consider whether keeping the property fits your next home purchase and your willingness to be a landlord.
Does the Rental Income Support the Property?

Start with what the property could realistically rent for in the local market, then compare that income with the full cost of ownership.

Estimate Rent Using Comparable Properties

Look at what similar homes are actually renting for in the local market. Compare properties with a similar location, size, condition, parking setup, and features. A rent estimate based on a different neighborhood or property type can make the numbers look better than they really are.

Include More Than the Mortgage Payment

Your mortgage is only one expense. Property taxes, insurance, HOA fees, repairs, landscaping, and utilities you agree to cover can continue after you move out. Large expenses matter, too. A roof, HVAC system, appliance, or plumbing repair can quickly change the numbers.

Leave Room for Vacancies and Turnover

A rental may not be occupied every month of every year. Tenants move, repairs happen, and a property may need cleaning or updates between leases. If the numbers only work when the home is occupied continuously, and nothing needs repair, there may not be enough room in the budget for normal rental-property expenses.

What Changes When a Primary Residence Becomes a Rental?

If you plan to turn your primary residence into a rental, the change can affect how the property is financed, insured, taxed, and managed.

Review Your Mortgage and Insurance

If the property has a mortgage, review the loan documents and contact the lender if you are unsure about occupancy requirements. Terms that applied while the property was your primary residence may not be the same after you move.

Insurance can change as well. Coverage designed for an owner-occupied home may not be suitable once tenants live there. Talk with your insurance provider before renting the property.

Check HOA and Local Rental Rules

If the home is part of an HOA, review any restrictions on leasing, minimum lease terms, tenant registration, or rental caps. State and local requirements may also apply to landlords and erties. Confirm the rules that apply to the property before advertising it for rent. rental prop

Understand the Tax Side

Rental income is generally taxable. Certain rental expenses may be deductible under applicable tax rules, and depreciation can also become part of the tax picture.

Converting a primary residence into a rental can affect the tax treatment of the property when it is eventually sold. Rules involving depreciation, ownership, use, and potential home-sale exclusions depend on the circumstances. Keep detailed records from the beginning, and consider speaking with a qualified tax professional before converting the home.

How Will Keeping the Home Affect Your Next Move?

Keeping the property means keeping its financial obligations while taking on the costs of your next home.

Consider Your Next Mortgage

A lender may be able to consider rental income under its guidelines, but the existing mortgage and other debts can still affect qualification. Speak with a lender before assuming expected rent will make the next purchase work. It is better to understand the financing before you begin shopping for another home.

Consider the Equity That Would Stay in the Property

Selling can release equity that may be useful for a down payment, moving costs, debt reduction, or another priority. If you keep the home, that equity remains tied to the property. Compare the value of keeping the rental with what selling could allow you to do next.

Do You Want the Responsibilities of Being a Landlord?

Someone has to market the property, screen prospective tenants, prepare the lease, collect rent, respond to maintenance requests, document the property’s condition, and follow applicable rental laws.

Managing the Property Yourself

You may be comfortable handling the work if you live nearby and have the time. Be realistic about after-hours repairs, tenant communication, recordkeeping, and the time needed between leases.

Hiring a Property Manager

If you are moving farther away or do not want the day-to-day responsibility, you may prefer a property manager. Include the expected management cost when you calculate whether keeping the home makes sense.

When Selling May Make More Sense

Selling your home may be the better option if keeping the property would add more cost, risk, or responsibility than it is likely to return.

Consider selling if:

The expected rent would not comfortably cover the property’s ongoing costs.
You need the home’s equity for your next purchase or another financial priority.
Major repairs or updates are likely in the near future.
You do not want the responsibility of managing tenants or paying for property management.
Keeping the property could make it harder to qualify for your next mortgage.
When Keeping the Home May Be Worth Exploring

If you want to keep your current home as a rental, start by checking whether local rental demand and expected rent can support the property’s ongoing costs. Leave room in the budget for vacancies, repairs, insurance, and property management if needed.

Keeping the home may make more sense when you have enough financial flexibility to handle unexpected costs, and you are comfortable managing the property or paying someone to do it. These factors do not guarantee that renting is the better choice, but they can help you decide whether the option is worth considering.

BROWSE LISTINGS
Frequently Asked Questions
Should I rent or sell my house when I move?

If you are deciding whether to rent out your old house or sell it, compare realistic rental income with the full cost of keeping the property. Also consider the equity you could access by selling, your next-home financing, tax implications, and whether you want landlord responsibilities.

Can I turn my primary residence into a rental?

In many cases, yes, but check your mortgage terms, insurance, HOA rules, and applicable state or local rental requirements first. You should also understand how converting the property to a rental may affect taxes when you eventually sell.

Is rental income taxable?

Generally, yes. Rental income is typically taxable, while certain qualifying expenses may be deductible. Tax treatment depends on the circumstances, so keep good records and consult a qualified tax professional when needed.

Choosing Between Renting and Selling

Keeping your current home as a rental can provide income, but it also adds costs, responsibilities, and financial risk. Run the numbers using realistic rent and expenses, then decide whether owning a rental property fits your finances and the way you want to manage your next move.

A local REMAX agent can help you compare the home’s potential sale price with local rental conditions. A lender, tax professional, insurance provider, and property manager can help with the parts of the decision outside the home sale itself.
