blog_posts.title: Seller Concessions: Limits and Rules for Buyers in 2026
blog_posts.text:
A seller concession is money the seller agrees to apply toward the buyer’s closing costs at settlement. The purchase price stays the same. The seller returns part of the proceeds to cover costs the buyer would otherwise bring in cash. Every major loan program caps how much a seller can contribute, and the cap depends on the loan type, the down payment and how the buyer will occupy the property. Most programs bar concessions from covering a down payment, and no concession can exceed the buyer’s actual closing costs.

Key takeaways
A seller concession pays the buyer’s closing costs. It is not a reduction in the contract price.
Lenders call these interested party contributions, or IPCs. The loan program sets the cap, not the buyer, seller or agent.
Conventional caps run from 2% to 9% of the price depending on down payment and occupancy. FHA and USDA cap at 6%. VA uses a split structure.
Most programs bar concessions from covering a down payment, financial reserves or cash back to the buyer.
A concession cannot exceed the buyer’s actual closing costs. Any unused portion does not convert to cash.
What is a seller concession?

A seller concession is a credit the buyer and seller negotiate and write into the purchase agreement. It appears on the closing disclosure as a seller-paid item and reduces the cash the buyer wires at settlement. The same arrangement goes by several names, including seller-paid closing costs, seller contributions and seller credits. Lenders use the term interested party contribution, which is broader. An interested party is anyone with a financial stake in the transaction, including the seller, the builder, the developer and the real estate brokerages involved. All contributions from all interested parties count against a single combined cap.

Both parties must disclose concessions to the lender. Undisclosed side agreements, such as an off-contract payment or an item of value the seller leaves behind for the buyer, can violate the loan terms.

What can a seller concession pay for?

Eligible costs are the ones a buyer normally pays at closing. Common items include:

Loan origination and underwriting fees
Discount points, including points used for a rate buydown
Appraisal and credit report fees
Title insurance, settlement and recording fees
Prepaid property taxes and homeowners insurance
Escrow account deposits
HOA dues, which conventional guidelines allow a buyer to prepay up to 12 months

Costs that generally do not qualify include the down payment, financial reserves required by the lender, personal property, furniture and moving expenses. Program rules differ on home warranties and repair credits, so those two items raise a lender question rather than follow a general rule.

How much can a seller contribute?

The loan program sets the cap and measures it against either the sale price or the appraised value, depending on the program. The figures below reflect published agency guidelines.

Interested party contribution limits by loan program. Caps are combined across all interested parties. Confirm current figures with a licensed mortgage professional.
LOAN TYPE	BUYER SITUATION	CONTRIBUTION CAP
Conventional	Primary or second home, less than 10% down	3%
Conventional	Primary or second home, 10% to 24.99% down	6%
Conventional	Primary or second home, 25% or more down	9%
Conventional	Investment property, any down payment	2%
FHA	All occupancy types	6%
USDA	Eligible rural properties	6%
VA	Eligible borrowers	Customary closing costs, plus 4% in concessions for specified items
How is a concession different from a price reduction?

The two move different numbers. A price reduction lowers the contract price, which lowers the loan amount, the down payment in dollars and the monthly principal and interest. It also becomes the recorded sale price used in future comparable sales. A concession leaves the contract price intact and reduces the cash the buyer needs on closing day.

Which one carries more value to a given buyer depends on whether that buyer is short on cash at the table or short on monthly room in the budget. That comparison runs through the loan file, so a lender and an agent are the two people positioned to run it.

How do buyers request a seller concession?
Confirm the cap first. Ask the lender for the maximum IPC on the specific loan program and down payment before a number goes in the offer.
Get an estimate of actual closing costs. The concession cannot exceed them, so a request above that figure has no effect.
Write it into the offer. Concessions are stated in the purchase agreement as a dollar amount or a percentage of the price.
Ask the agent for local context. An agent can pull what concessions were recorded on comparable closings in the same market and price band.
Treat it as one term among several. Price, closing timeline, contingencies and possession all sit on the same negotiation.
What limits a concession at closing?

Four things narrow the number. The program cap sets the ceiling. Actual closing costs set a second ceiling, since the credit cannot exceed them. The appraisal matters because several programs calculate the cap against the lesser of the sale price or the appraised value. And the down payment restriction applies across most programs, so concession dollars cannot be redirected to cover it.

A local agent can walk through how concessions are typically structured in a specific market and price range.

When is a concession finalized?

A concession is negotiated in the purchase agreement, but it is not settled at that point. The lender reviews it during underwriting against the program cap and against the buyer’s actual closing costs, and either figure can pull the number down. What governs at the table is the amount shown on the closing disclosure, which federal rules require the buyer to receive at least three business days before closing.

That timing has a practical effect. A concession renegotiated late in the transaction, after an inspection or an appraisal for example, can require a revised closing disclosure and restart the three-day waiting period. Agents and lenders generally surface concession changes as early as the facts allow for that reason.

BROWSE LISTINGS
Frequently asked questions
What is a seller concession?

A seller concession is money the seller agrees to apply toward the buyer’s closing costs at settlement. The contract price does not change. The credit appears on the closing disclosure and reduces the cash the buyer brings to closing. Lenders refer to these as interested party contributions.

What is the maximum seller concession on a conventional loan?

Conventional caps depend on down payment and occupancy. For a primary or second home, the cap is 3% with less than 10% down, 6% with 10% to 24.99% down and 9% with 25% or more down. Investment properties are capped at 2% regardless of down payment.

Can seller concessions be used for a down payment?

No. Fannie Mae states that interested party contributions cannot be applied to the down payment, financial reserves or the borrower’s minimum required contribution. Other programs carry similar restrictions. Concessions apply to closing costs and prepaid items only.

Do seller concessions lower the purchase price?

No. The contract price stays the same and is the figure recorded as the sale price. A concession reduces the buyer’s cash requirement at closing rather than the amount financed.

Can a seller concession pay for a mortgage rate buydown?

Discount points are an eligible closing cost on most programs, so concession funds can be applied to a buydown. The cost of the buydown counts against the same contribution cap as every other seller-paid item. A lender can confirm eligibility for a specific loan program.

What happens if the concession exceeds the buyer’s closing costs?

The excess does not go to the buyer as cash. Depending on the program and the amount, the credit is reduced to match actual costs, or the contract is amended. Contributions above program limits can require a dollar-for-dollar reduction in the price used to calculate the maximum loan amount.

Who counts as an interested party?

An interested party is anyone with a financial stake in the transaction, including the seller, the builder, the developer and the real estate brokerages involved. Contributions from all interested parties are combined and measured against a single cap.

blog_posts.title: How to Sell a House in a Flood Zone
blog_posts.text:
Selling a house in a flood zone is possible, but buyers want more information before they feel comfortable moving forward. Flood maps, insurance, financing, and any known flood history can all become part of the conversation. The best approach is to confirm the property’s current flood information, organize the records you already have, and be clear about what is known. A FEMA flood designation describes mapped risk. It does not mean a particular home will flood, and homes outside mapped high-risk areas can still experience flooding.

Key Takeaways
Check the property’s current FEMA flood map before listing.
Flood insurance requirements can vary by flood zone and lender.
Disclosure rules differ by state and locality, so known flood history should be handled carefully.
Keep repair, mitigation, elevation, and insurance records organized for buyers.
Price the home using relevant local comparable sales rather than assuming every flood-zone property requires the same discount.
Confirm the Current FEMA Flood Map

FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Maps identify flood hazard areas in participating communities. Because maps can change as studies and mapping data are updated, confirm the current information before you list. A Special Flood Hazard Area generally covers land with at least a 1% chance of flooding in any given year and includes designated A and V zones. The FEMA Flood Map Service Center is the official public source for flood map information. If the designation is unclear, a local floodplain professional or surveyor may be able to help interpret the property’s situation.

Understand How Flood Risk Can Affect Financing

Flood-zone status can matter to a buyer’s lender. For certain federally regulated or insured loans secured by property in a Special Flood Hazard Area, flood insurance may be required. The buyer’s lender determines the requirements for that loan.

That means insurance cost can become part of the buyer’s affordability calculation. It is better for a buyer to investigate that cost early than discover it close to closing. If you already carry flood insurance, you can make the policy information available as background, but do not assume the buyer will receive the same premium.

Disclose Flood History Carefully

Flood disclosure rules vary by state and locality. Sellers may have obligations related to known flooding, flood damage, drainage issues, insurance claims, or other property conditions.

If the home has flooded before, explain what happened and what work was completed afterward. Gather available records, such as insurance claims, photos, remediation reports, contractor invoices, permits, and documentation for repairs or mitigation work.

Complete required disclosures accurately, and avoid minimizing known issues. Buyers can then review the information with their inspector, insurer, or other advisers. Legal questions about what must be disclosed should be directed to the appropriate professional or local authority.

Document Any Flood-Mitigation Work

Some homes have improvements intended to reduce damage or manage water more effectively. For instance, waterfront homes may include elevation work, flood vents, drainage changes, sump systems, backflow prevention, relocated utilities, or grading improvements.

Keep permits, engineering records, and invoices for completed work. If you have an Elevation Certificate, or a FEMA Letter of Map Amendment or Revision, make that available. These documents can provide useful context, but they should be described accurately rather than used to suggest that a property has no flood risk.

Price Against the Right Comparable Sales

There is no standard percentage that every flood-zone home should be discounted. Market impact varies with location, flood history, insurance costs, mitigation, condition and buyer demand.

The strongest pricing discussion starts with local comparable sales. Comparable sales should also reflect similar flood-risk characteristics whenever possible, rather than comparing only homes outside the flood zone. When possible, consider homes with similar flood-risk characteristics as well as similar size, condition, and location. A local agent can help identify which sales are meaningful and which ones are likely to create a misleading comparison.

Market the Home Honestly

Good real estate marketing can highlight the home’s genuine strengths without hiding the flood zone. Location, updates, layout, views, outdoor areas, and documented mitigation work can all be relevant. Avoid phrases such as “flood-proof” or “no flood risk.” Flood maps describe risk, and FEMA notes that flooding can occur outside mapped high-risk areas. A buyer who receives accurate information early is less likely to feel surprised later in the transaction.

Expect Insurance Questions

A serious buyer may contact an insurance professional before making an offer or during due diligence. That is sensible because insurance can affect the ongoing cost of owning the property.

Buyers Should Get Their Own Insurance Quote

Share the records you have, but let the buyer obtain their own quote. Coverage choices, rating factors, and the buyer’s circumstances may differ from yours.

Confirm Whether an Existing Policy Can Be Transferred

If you believe an existing policy can be transferred, confirm that directly with the insurer rather than presenting it as a certainty.

BROWSE LISTINGS
Frequently Asked Questions
Can you sell a house in a flood zone?

Yes. Homes in flood zones are bought and sold regularly. Flood designation can affect insurance, financing, buyer demand, and due diligence, so accurate information and early preparation are important.

Does a buyer need flood insurance?

It depends on the property, flood zone, and financing. Certain loans on properties in Special Flood Hazard Areas require flood insurance. Buyers should confirm the requirement with their lender and insurance professional.

What if my house flooded in the past?

Review the disclosure rules that apply where the property is located and organize records of the event, repairs, and mitigation. Buyers may want their own inspections and professional advice before moving forward.

Preparing for a Flood-Zone Home Sale

Selling a house in a flood zone calls for preparation, not dramatic language. Confirm the map, be clear about the property’s known history, and give buyers enough information to evaluate the risk for themselves.

Updated September 16, 2026

As of its September 15-16, 2026 meeting, the Federal Reserve announced that it is raising the federal funds rate by a quarter percentage point, to 3.75% to 4%. This is the sixth rate announcement of 2026 and the first rate change of the year. The previous five announcements, in January, March, April, June and July, all left the rate unchanged. The decision came after the Federal Open Market Committee’s September meeting.

The federal funds rate is the rate banks charge each other for overnight lending. It is not a mortgage rate, and mortgage rates do not automatically move with it.

According to the Federal Reserve’s press release, the FOMC approved the statement by a 12-0 vote and decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 3.75% to 4%. There were no dissenting votes. At the July meeting, three members dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase: Beth M. Hammack, Neel Kashkari and Lorie K. Logan.

The FOMC statement described economic activity as expanding at a solid pace and said domestic spending has been resilient, while noting that uncertainty remains elevated owing in part to geopolitical developments. The statement described productivity growth as strong and capital investment as robust. It said job gains have kept pace with the workforce and that the unemployment rate has changed little. The committee stated that inflation remains elevated and that the rate increase will support a timelier return to its 2 percent goal.

The committee also stated that it is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system. This was Chair Kevin Warsh’s third FOMC meeting as chairman, following Jerome Powell’s departure in May. As at the June and July meetings, the post-meeting statement was shorter than what had become standard practice.

What the Federal Funds Rate Does and Does Not Control

The federal funds rate is the target range the FOMC sets for the rate depository institutions charge one another for overnight loans. It influences short-term borrowing costs across the economy, including credit cards, auto loans and home equity lines of credit, which are commonly tied to the prime rate.

Long-term mortgage rates work differently. The 30-year fixed mortgage rate tracks the 10-year Treasury yield more closely than it tracks the federal funds rate. Treasury yields respond to bond market demand, inflation expectations and investor appetite for risk. A Fed rate change is one input among several rather than a direct lever on what a buyer is quoted.

The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meets eight times a year and announces its decision on what to do with the benchmark interest rate. The schedule for 2026 is as follows:

The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 12 – 0 vote:

The Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve’s dual mandate. The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.

Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.

Inflation remains elevated. Today’s policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability.

What is the Benchmark Interest Rate and What Does it Mean for Homebuyers and Homeowners?

Interest rate decisions can have a direct impact on your wallet. When buying a home, most people need to borrow the required funds in the form of a mortgage. The mortgage interest rate refers to the percentage a borrower pays to a lender on the funds borrowed for the purchase. Your lender determines your interest rate based on factors including credit risk, loan type and market conditions.

Your mortgage rate is not the same as the benchmark rate. The federal funds rate is set by the Federal Open Market Committee at its scheduled meetings and shapes short-term borrowing costs across the economy. Mortgage rates respond mainly to the 10-year Treasury yield and to lender-specific factors including your debt-to-income ratio and credit score.

Understanding how rate decisions flow through to mortgage pricing can help you plan a purchase. More guidance for buyers is in the Home Buyer’s Hub. When you are ready to start home hunting, your REMAX agent will be there to help guide you.

The federal funds rate is the target range the Federal Open Market Committee sets for the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Fed does not set consumer loan rates directly. It sets this benchmark, and other rates respond to it in varying degrees.

Does a Fed rate hike raise mortgage rates?

Not automatically. The 30-year fixed mortgage rate follows the 10-year Treasury yield more closely than the federal funds rate. Treasury yields move on inflation expectations, bond market demand and investor sentiment. Mortgage rates have moved in the opposite direction from an FOMC decision in past cycles.

Short-term and variable-rate borrowing responds most closely, including credit cards, home equity lines of credit and auto loans. Many of these are tied to the prime rate, which generally moves with the federal funds rate.

The FOMC statement said inflation remains elevated and that the rate increase will support a timelier return to the committee’s 2 percent goal. blog_posts.text:
Watch: July’s market in 40 seconds

The REMAX National Housing Report tracks how long homes take to sell across 46 metro areas each month. In July 2026 the average home spent 45 days on market, three days longer than in June and one day longer than a year earlier. That national figure covered a wide range, from metros where homes went under contract in under three weeks to one where the typical listing took nearly three months.

Days on market measures the time between when a home is listed and when the seller signs a contract. A lower number points to faster turnover and, in most cases, steadier buyer demand relative to supply. The rankings below show where homes sold quickest and where they sat longest in July 2026.

BROWSE LISTINGS

Key Takeaways
The national average was 45 days on market in July 2026, up three days from June.
Hartford, CT recorded the fastest sales at 18 days.
San Antonio, TX recorded the slowest at 85 days, nearly five times Hartford’s pace.
All five of the slowest markets were in the Sun Belt.
Speed did not track price. Fast and slow markets appeared across a range of price points.
Where Did Homes Sell Fastest in July 2026?

According to the National Housing Report, Hartford, Connecticut had the shortest average time on market in July 2026 at 18 days. Omaha, Nebraska and Anchorage, Alaska followed, tied at 25 days, then Cincinnati, Ohio at 26 days and Chicago, Illinois at 27 days. Each of these markets moved at least 18 days faster than the national average of 45.

Hartford has held one of the tightest markets in the report for months, with among the lowest supply of homes for sale of any metro surveyed. When listings are scarce relative to buyers, homes tend to sell quickly, and Connecticut’s capital showed that pattern clearly in July.

2 (tie)	Omaha, NE	25
2 (tie)	Anchorage, AK	25

Where Did Homes Sell Slowest in July 2026?

San Antonio, Texas had the longest average time on market at 85 days. Miami, Florida followed at 77 days, then Phoenix, Arizona at 74 days, Tampa, Florida at 71 days and Orlando, Florida at 65 days. All five sat well above the national average of 45.

Each of these markets also carried more homes for sale than the country as a whole. San Antonio and Miami held some of the largest months’ supply figures in the July report, which gave buyers more to choose from and less reason to rush a decision.

Rank	Metro Area	Avg. Days on Market (July 2026)
1	San Antonio, TX	85
2	Miami, FL	77

4	Tampa, FL	71

What Explained the Gap in July 2026?

The spread between the fastest and slowest markets came down largely to the balance between supply and demand in each metro. Markets in the Northeast and Midwest, including Hartford, Cincinnati and Chicago, entered July with limited inventory, so homes that came up for sale met ready buyers. Several Sun Belt metros carried heavier inventory after years of construction and in-migration, which lengthened the time a typical listing stayed active.

Season played a part too. July sits past the spring peak, and the national average lengthened by three days from June as summer sales cooled. Homes still sold, just at a more measured pace than during the busiest months of the year.

What Did This Mean for Buyers and Sellers?

Days on market describes an entire metro, not a single neighborhood or home. A well-priced listing in a slow market can still sell in days, and an overpriced one in a fast market can sit. In quicker metros like Hartford or Cincinnati, buyers benefited from pre-approval and fast decisions. In slower metros like San Antonio or Tampa, buyers generally had more time to compare homes and negotiate. blog_posts.text:
July 2026 Housing Market Update: What Buyers and Sellers Should Know

Buyers had more to choose from in July 2026 as inventory rose from both the previous month and a year ago, while prices held flat month over month across the 46 metro areas surveyed. The national median sales price was $450,000, up 3.4% from July 2025, and buyers paid an average of 99% of asking price. Home sales slipped from June but still finished ahead of last year. Here is what the latest REMAX National Housing Report says about July 2026 home prices, sales and inventory, and what it means for buyers and sellers.

Key Takeaways
Home sales fell 5.7% from June but were up 2.5% from July 2025.
The median sales price held at $450,000, flat from June and up 3.4% from a year ago.
New listings rose 1.4% year over year but were down 2.7% from June.
Total inventory grew 2.8% from June and 4.7% from July 2025.
Homes sold in 45 days on average, three days slower than June and one day slower than last July.
Months’ supply of inventory was 3.0 and the average close-to-list price ratio held at 99%.

Watch: July’s market in 40 seconds

What Happened to Home Sales in July?

Home sales slipped 5.7% from June but held 2.5% above July 2025, a sign of steady year-over-year demand even as monthly activity cooled. Results ranged widely by metro. Bozeman, MT led annual sales growth at 22.9%, followed by Wichita, KS at 13.4%, Honolulu, HI at 11.9%, Miami, FL at 11.8% and Minneapolis, MN at 11.6%. The biggest annual declines came in Raleigh, NC, down 7.3%, followed by Birmingham, AL, down 4.9% and Houston, TX, down 3.9%.

Miami stood out, with closed sales up 11.8% from a year ago and a spot among the top five metros for annual growth. Anthony Askowitz, Broker/Owner of REMAX Advance Realty in Miami, described his market this way: “This month’s data reflects the ever-changing real estate market in Miami. We had more sales in July as buyers found opportunities across a wider range of price points. Sellers are also becoming savvier and understand that they need to price appropriately if they don’t want their property to sit on the market. As agents, our focus remains on educating buyers and sellers on today’s market reality and what to expect in a given price range.”

How Did July 2026 Home Prices Move?

The national median sales price was $450,000 in July 2026, flat from June and up 3.4% from July 2025. The median listing price of newly listed homes was down 1.1% from June and up 1.8% year over year, which points to steady rather than accelerating price growth. The biggest annual gains came in Trenton, NJ, up 8.1% to $574,500, Pittsburgh, PA, up 7.3% to $279,000 and New York, NY, up 6.1% to $700,000. A few markets saw prices ease, led by Bozeman, MT, down 12.6% to $690,000, Wichita, KS, down 3.8% to $250,000 and San Antonio, TX, down 3.2% to $319,000. For sellers, flat national pricing supports realistic listing expectations. For buyers, the numbers suggest waiting for broad price drops may not pay off in most markets.

What Happened to New Listings?

New listings rose 1.4% compared with July 2025 but dipped 2.7% from June. The annual gain gives buyers a slightly larger pool of fresh options in many metros. The biggest year-over-year increases came in Anchorage, AK at 21.6%, St. Louis, MO at 12.3% and Indianapolis, IN at 10.7%, with Providence, RI and Minneapolis, MN close behind. The sharpest pullbacks were in San Antonio, TX at 11.3%, Baltimore, MD at 8.1% and San Diego, CA at 5.7%.

Is There Enough Inventory for Buyers?

Total inventory rose 2.8% from June and 4.7% from July 2025, continuing a stretch of measured rather than dramatic supply growth. Months’ supply of inventory came in at 3.0, up from 2.7 in June and 2.9 in July 2025. A reading around three months sits near the line between a buyer’s and a seller’s market. The most buyer-friendly markets by months’ supply were Miami, FL at 6.2, San Antonio, TX at 6.0 and Houston, TX at 5.2, with Los Angeles, CA and San Diego, CA both above 4.5. The tightest markets were Hartford, CT at 0.9, Albuquerque, NM at 1.3 and Philadelphia, PA at 1.4, followed by St. Louis, MO and Tulsa, OK at 1.5.

How Fast Did Homes Sell in July 2026?

Homes sold in an average of 45 days, three days slower than June and one day slower than July 2025. The quickest markets were Hartford, CT at 18 days, Omaha, NE at 25 days and Anchorage, AK at 25 days, with Cincinnati, OH and Chicago, IL close behind. The slowest were San Antonio, TX at 85 days, Miami, FL at 77 days and Phoenix, AZ at 74 days. In the fastest metros, buyers who delay risk losing the right home to another offer, which makes pre-approval and quick decisions valuable.

How Close to Asking Price Are Buyers Paying?

The average close-to-list price ratio was 99%, unchanged from both June and July 2025. A ratio above 100% means homes sold for more than the list price. San Francisco, CA led at 105.2%, followed by Hartford, CT at 104.7%, New York, NY at 102.4% and Trenton, NJ at 101.4%. Buyers found the most room to negotiate in Miami, FL at 94.4%, Tampa, FL at 97.0% and Houston, TX at 97.1%.

What Does the July 2026 Market Mean for Buyers and Sellers?

For buyers, inventory keeps building and months’ supply crossed 3.0, which means more choice than earlier in the year, though the fastest metros still reward decisive offers. Getting pre-approved and working with an agent who knows local pricing helps buyers move with confidence.

For sellers, accurate pricing carries the most weight. Well-priced homes are still drawing demand, while overpriced listings risk sitting as more inventory comes online. Conditions range from 0.9 months’ supply in Hartford to 6.2 in Miami, so a local REMAX agent can read these conditions market by market and build a plan that fits.

The national median sales price in July 2026 was $450,000, flat from June 2026 and up 3.4% from July 2025, according to the REMAX National Housing Report.

Home sales fell 5.7% from June to July 2026 but were up 2.5% compared with July 2025. Most of the 46 metro areas surveyed still posted annual gains.

New listings rose 1.4% year over year in July 2026, though they dipped 2.7% from June. Total inventory grew 2.8% from June and 4.7% from a year ago.

Homes sold in an average of 45 days in July 2026, three days slower than June and one day slower than July 2025.

With 3.0 months’ supply of inventory and an average close-to-list ratio of 99%, most metros sat near balanced in July 2026, with a slight edge to sellers. Conditions vary widely, from 0.9 months’ supply in Hartford, CT to 6.2 in Miami, FL.

Where Home Prices Sit Furthest Below the National Median

The national median sales price reached $460,000 in June 2026, according to the REMAX National Housing Report. In a long list of major metros, however, the typical home costs $100,000 to $200,000 less than that. The rankings below draw on metro-level median sales prices from the REMAX National Housing Report, using May 2026 figures, the most recent complete metro data, along with June updates where the report published them.

Key Takeaways
Cleveland, OH and Wichita, KS tied for the lowest median sales price among major metros at $260,000, roughly $200,000 below the June national median.
Ten major metros posted median prices under $330,000.
Affordable does not always mean easy. Cleveland, Cincinnati and St. Louis homes sold in about a month or less at or above list price.
San Antonio and New Orleans combined low prices with the most negotiating room, with months’ supply near five or higher.
Pittsburgh posted one of the biggest annual price gains in the June report even while staying under $300,000.
The 10 Most Affordable Major Housing Markets
1. Cleveland, OH – $260,000 (tie)

Cleveland tied for the lowest median sales price in the report at $260,000. Low prices did not slow demand. Homes sold in an average of 25 days at 100% of list price, with just 1.3 months’ supply of inventory.

2. Wichita, KS – $260,000 (tie)

Wichita matched Cleveland at $260,000 with a somewhat calmer pace. Homes averaged 40 days on market with 2.0 months’ supply and a 99% close-to-list ratio, a calmer pace than most other low-priced metros in the report posted.

3. Pittsburgh, PA – $290,000

Pittsburgh’s June 2026 median of $290,000 was up 6.4% from a year earlier, one of the five biggest annual gains in the June report. New listings also jumped 13.8% year over year in June, tied for the third largest increase among the metros surveyed, which added fresh options in one of the country’s most affordable major markets.

4. New Orleans, LA – $300,000

New Orleans paired a $300,000 median with some of the most buyer-friendly conditions in the report: 4.9 months’ supply, 61 average days on market and a 97% close-to-list ratio. Few metros in the report combined affordability with that much supply.

5. Detroit, MI – $305,000

Detroit’s $305,000 median came with serious momentum. The metro led the entire June report in annual sales growth, with closed transactions up 26.1% from June 2025. Homes sold in about 28 days with 1.8 months’ supply.

6. St. Louis, MO – $307,250

St. Louis posted a $307,250 median and a 101% close-to-list ratio, meaning the typical home sold above asking. With 34 average days on market and 1.3 months’ supply, listings moved quickly.

7. San Antonio, TX – $310,950

San Antonio offered the most leverage of any affordable metro. In June, homes averaged 86 days on market, the longest in the report, with 5.5 months’ supply, the second highest. A $310,950 median plus a 97% close-to-list ratio completed the most buyer-leaning data profile among the affordable metros.

8. Des Moines, IA – $315,000

Des Moines combined a $315,000 median with a supply boost. New listings rose 16.2% year over year in June, the second biggest increase in the report. Homes averaged 56 days on market with 2.6 months’ supply.

9. Indianapolis, IN – $324,945

Indianapolis came in at $324,945 with 36 average days on market, 1.7 months’ supply and a 99% close-to-list ratio, a balanced picture that leans slightly toward sellers.

10. Cincinnati, OH – $328,798

Cincinnati rounded out the list at $328,798 and ranked among the fastest markets anywhere. Homes sold in 24 days on average in June, one of the five quickest paces in the report, at 100% of list price with 1.3 months’ supply. Affordable, yes. Slow, no.

What Affordable Markets Have in Common

Two patterns stood out. First, the most affordable metros clustered in the Midwest and South, where median prices ran 30% to 45% below the national figure. Second, low prices came with fast competition. Cleveland, Cincinnati, St. Louis and Detroit all posted less than two months’ supply, and several closed at or above asking. The exceptions were San Antonio and New Orleans, where higher supply gave buyers more room. Price alone never tells the whole story, which is why an agent with local market knowledge matters as much in a $260,000 market as in a $1 million one.

Learning how to create a study area comes down to four things: natural light, seating that holds up through long sessions, storage that keeps supplies contained and a spot where noise stays low. Those four matter more than square footage. A corner of a bedroom can outperform a dedicated office when the light is good and the clutter has somewhere to go.

The same four checks work while touring houses, because a floor plan either offers a workable study spot or it does not. Here is what each element does, and what to look for in a home before the school year starts.

Key takeaways
Natural light is the hardest element to add later, so window placement should drive where the desk goes.
Seating with arms and back support keeps homework sessions from ending early.
Closed storage such as woven baskets keeps supplies within reach without making the room look like a classroom.
A quiet zone can be carved out of an underused corner, landing or spare bedroom.
Buyers can evaluate study potential on a showing by checking light, outlets, wall space and sound.
Why does natural lighting matter in a study area?

Natural light reduces the eye strain that comes from staring at a screen under a single overhead fixture, and it makes a small space feel usable rather than boxed in. A desk positioned near a window gives the eyes something distant to focus on between tasks, which is part of the standard 20-20-20 guidance eye doctors give screen users.

Placement does most of the work. A desk set perpendicular to a window brings light across the work surface instead of straight into the screen, which cuts glare without giving up the view. North-facing windows deliver steady light through the day. South-facing windows deliver more of it but need a sheer shade or blind to stay comfortable in the afternoon.

Light is also the element that is hardest to add after the fact. Paint colors change in a weekend. Furniture gets swapped. Adding a window means cutting into structure, pulling permits and hiring a contractor. That is why window placement should be the first thing considered when picking the room, and why it belongs on a buyer’s list during showings.

What kind of seating works best for a home study area?

Seating decides how long anyone actually stays in the study area. A chair that looks good and feels wrong after 20 minutes turns into a chair nobody uses, and the homework migrates back to the kitchen table. Support matters more than style.

For desk work, look for a seat height that lets feet rest flat on the floor with knees at roughly a 90 degree angle, and a back that meets the lower spine rather than curving away from it. Arms help during reading and tablet use by taking weight off the shoulders. An upholstered accent chair with a solid wood frame handles the reading half of studying well, while a task chair with adjustable height handles the typing half. Many households end up using both, with the desk chair for focused work and a softer seat nearby for reading.

Scale is the piece people miss. A deep lounge chair swallows a small room and pushes the desk into a corner. Measuring the chair footprint before buying keeps the walkway clear and keeps the room from feeling crowded.

How does smart storage keep a study area usable?

Storage is what keeps a study area from turning back into a drop zone by October. Supplies multiply fast during the school year, and a surface covered in paper stops functioning as a work surface. The fix is giving every category a container and putting that container within arm’s reach of the desk.

Woven baskets do this well because they close the loop between function and appearance. A large basket handles blankets, backpacks and anything bulky. Smaller lidded boxes handle pens, chargers and calculators. Vertical storage adds capacity without taking floor space, so a wall shelf above the desk or a slim bookcase beside it clears the desktop for actual work.

A simple rule keeps the system running: anything used daily stays on the desk, anything used weekly goes in a basket or drawer and anything used a few times a year moves to a closet. Reviewing the setup at each grading period takes about ten minutes and prevents the slow creep of clutter that ends most homework stations.

How do you create a quiet work area in a busy house?

Quiet is a design problem, not a luck problem. Sound travels through open sightlines and hard surfaces, so the goal is to break both. Position the desk so it faces away from the main traffic path through the house. Add soft material: a rug underfoot, curtains at the window and an upholstered chair all absorb sound that hard floors and bare walls bounce around.

Households often need two quiet zones rather than one. Kids need somewhere to study, and working parents need somewhere to take calls. Splitting them across floors or across the house keeps a video meeting from colliding with a math lesson. A spare bedroom, a wide landing, a finished basement corner or a section of a formal dining room that goes unused most of the year can all absorb the second zone.

The need is common. U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey data puts the share of workers who worked from home at 13.3 percent in 2024, compared with 13.8 percent in 2023 and 5.7 percent in 2019. A home that can hold both a study area and a work area serves a wider range of households than one that can hold only a desk.

What should buyers look for when touring homes?

Study space is easy to evaluate on a showing once the four elements become a checklist. Walk each candidate room and check the following.

Light. Note which direction the windows face and whether a desk could sit near one without blocking a door or a walkway.
Outlets. Count them and note where they sit. A room with one outlet behind the door will need an electrician or a visible extension cord.
Wall space. Look for at least one uninterrupted stretch wide enough for a desk. Rooms with a door, a closet and a window on three walls often have less usable space than the square footage suggests.
Sound. Stand in the room and listen. Proximity to the laundry room, the garage or the main stairwell affects how quiet the space stays.
Connectivity. Ask about internet service and check whether the router location can reach the far corners of the house.

Sellers can work the same list in reverse. Staging a spare room as a defined study area gives buyers a use for a room that might otherwise read as leftover space, and it photographs well in listing images. A desk, a chair, a lamp and a shelf communicate function faster than an empty room does.

A local REMAX agent can point out which floor plans in a given market tend to include flexible rooms, which neighborhoods have the internet infrastructure to support remote work and how a staged study area affects buyer response in that area. Connect with a REMAX agent to start the search.

Frequently asked questions
How much space does a study area need?

A functional study area needs roughly 30 to 40 square feet, which covers a desk of about 48 inches wide, a chair and clearance to push back from the desk. Nooks, wide landings and closet conversions frequently meet that footprint without requiring a dedicated room.

Where is the best place to put a desk for natural light?

Perpendicular to the window is the general rule. That angle brings daylight across the work surface without putting glare on the screen or a bright window directly behind a video call. Facing a window directly can create screen glare, and sitting with the window at your back can wash out a camera image.

Can a study area be added to a room that already has another use?

Yes. Guest rooms, dining rooms and finished basements commonly host study areas. Defining the zone visually with a rug, a shelf or a change in lighting helps the space read as a separate area even when it shares a room with another function.

Does a home office or study area add value to a home?

A defined work space affects how buyers perceive a home’s flexibility, particularly in areas with a high share of remote workers. Whether it changes the appraised value depends on whether the space is a finished, permitted room or a staged corner. A local agent can explain how comparable homes in the area have been received.

What storage works best for a small study area?

Vertical and closed storage. Wall shelves and slim bookcases add capacity without consuming floor space, and lidded boxes or woven baskets keep supplies accessible while hiding visual clutter. Grouping items by how often they are used keeps the most-needed supplies closest to the desk.

blog_posts.title: Back-to-School Home Setup: 4 Functional Family Zones
blog_posts.text:
Getting a home ready for the school year works best around four functional zones: a dedicated work zone for kids, smart storage that keeps daily clutter out of sight, a quiet office for working parents and a mudroom that catches gear at the door. Each one solves a specific problem that shows up once schedules fill back up. The same spaces matter whether a family is settling into a current home, shopping for a new one before the year starts or preparing a home to sell, since functional layouts read as value on both sides of a move. The zones below cover what to include, where to put it and what each space signals to buyers and sellers.

Key Takeaways
A dedicated homework zone with good light and supplies within reach helps kids settle into schoolwork faster
Closed cabinets and labeled baskets keep everyday clutter out of sight and cut down on cleanup
A quiet, closed-door office supports video calls and focused work for parents on hybrid schedules
A mudroom or entry bench with hooks and bins turns the daily pile of backpacks and shoes into a system
Functional spaces like a home office and built-in storage rank among the features family buyers look for
For families moving around the school calendar, these zones double as a buyer’s checklist and a seller’s staging guide
Why does a dedicated work zone help kids stay focused?

A work zone that belongs to schoolwork and nothing else gives kids a clear signal that it is time to focus. The setup does not need to be large. A small desk, a comfortable chair and supplies within arm’s reach cover the basics for most ages.

Position the desk near natural light but out of the main flow of foot traffic, so the space stays quiet during study time. Keep pens, paper, chargers and calculators in a desktop caddy or labeled bins so nothing derails a homework session with a hunt for supplies. A shelf holds textbooks and reference materials, and a small board or wall calendar keeps assignment due dates in view.

Chair height matters more than it looks. Match the seat to the desk so posture holds up through longer reading and writing sessions, which keeps kids at the desk instead of drifting to the couch.

How does smart storage keep daily clutter out of sight?

Clutter builds fast once school schedules, activities and paperwork stack up. Smart storage gives every item a defined home, which keeps surfaces clear and makes cleanup a quick reset rather than a project.

Closed cabinets and drawers handle anything that does not need to be on display, from supplies and cords to seasonal gear. Open shelves work best for a curated mix of books and a few decorative pieces, since open storage reads as clutter the moment it gets crowded. Labeled baskets keep shared supplies sorted and easy for the whole family to reach without asking where things live.

A dedicated drop zone for papers earns its space during the school year. Permission slips, order forms and anything that needs a signature land in one spot instead of scattering across the kitchen counter. Built-in storage under a window seat or bench doubles the usefulness of a small footprint.

What makes a good quiet office for working parents?

Hybrid and remote schedules put video calls and deep focus into the daily routine, which makes a private work space worth carving out. A quiet office keeps work separate from household noise and gives parents a professional backdrop for meetings.

A room with a door that closes is the ideal, since it handles both call audio and concentration. When a separate room is not available, a corner with a room divider or a well-placed bookshelf can define the space. Position the desk so the background reads clean and uncluttered on camera, which matters for client-facing and internal calls alike.

Lighting does a lot of the work. A task lamp covers early mornings and late afternoons when natural light runs short, and a light source facing the desk reads better on video than a window behind it. A dedicated charging spot keeps laptops, headsets and phones ready at the start of each day.

Why does a mudroom matter during the school year?

Backpacks, shoes and sports gear pile up by the door within the first week of school. A mudroom or entry bench turns that daily pile into a system, which keeps the rest of the home cleaner and cuts down on the morning search for missing items.

Hooks installed at kid height let children hang backpacks and coats without help, which builds a routine they can manage on their own. A bench with storage underneath holds shoes, cleats and boots, and keeps the floor clear. Giving each family member a labeled bin or cubby prevents the daily mix-up over whose gear is whose.

A basket by the door handles anything heading back to school, from library books to signed forms and lunch containers. Placing it in the exit path means fewer forgotten items and fewer trips back inside. Durable, wipeable surfaces hold up to the mess that comes with busy family life.

What do these zones mean for buying or selling a home?

Back-to-school season overlaps with one of the busier stretches of the housing calendar, since many families aim to move before the school year begins. That timing makes functional spaces relevant on both sides of a transaction.

For buyers, these zones work as a practical checklist. A home office, built-in storage and an organized entry are hard to add after the fact, so a home that already has them or the flexibility to create them saves time and renovation cost. Flexible rooms that can shift from a study zone to a guest space or an office read as usable square footage rather than single-purpose rooms, which is worth weighing during a search.

For sellers, the same spaces are worth showcasing. Staging a spare room as a clear home office, clearing storage so cabinets and closets show their capacity, and keeping an entry organized all help a home present the way family buyers picture their own routine. A local REMAX agent can point out which of these features carry the most weight in a given market and how to position them when it is time to list.

An organized home makes the school year easier for the whole family, and the same spaces that reduce daily friction tend to hold their appeal on the market. Whether the goal is settling into a current home, buying a new one or getting ready to sell, a local REMAX agent can help match a home’s layout to the way a family actually lives.

Frequently Asked Questions
How do you set up a homework space for kids?

Choose a spot with good natural light, out of the main flow of foot traffic. Add a desk sized to the child, a chair at matching height, and supplies within reach in a caddy or labeled bins. A shelf for books and a board for due dates round out a work zone that helps kids focus.

What is the best storage for back-to-school clutter?

Closed cabinets and drawers work best for anything that does not need to be on display, while labeled baskets keep shared supplies sorted and easy to reach. A dedicated drop zone for papers keeps permission slips and forms in one place instead of scattered across counters.

Do you need a separate room for a home office?

A room with a door that closes is ideal for call audio and concentration, but it is not required. A corner defined by a room divider or bookshelf can work, as long as the desk faces a clean background for video calls and has good task lighting.

What is a mudroom used for?

A mudroom is a landing zone near an entry that catches backpacks, shoes, sports gear and daily mess. Hooks at kid height, a bench with storage underneath and labeled bins keep the space organized and the rest of the home cleaner during busy family routines.

Do functional spaces matter when buying or selling a home?

Yes. A home office, built-in storage and an organized entry are features family buyers look for and hard to add after the fact, so they work as a buyer’s checklist and a seller’s staging priority. A local REMAX agent can advise on which features carry the most weight in a given market.

blog_posts.title: Buying a Home for Football Season: A Fan’s Game Plan
blog_posts.text:
The short version: A home built for football season is decided by layout, not size. One uninterrupted wall for a screen, seating that all faces it, a kitchen with a sightline into the room, a bathroom on the entertaining level, enough outlets and broadband for a full house and parking for several cars. Nearly all of it can be checked in a 30 minute showing.

The 2026 NFL regular season opens Wednesday, September 9, when the Seattle Seahawks host the New England Patriots at Lumen Field in a rematch of Super Bowl LX. Week 1 runs through September 14, the regular season ends January 10, 2027 and Super Bowl LXI is scheduled for February 14, 2027 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

For a household that hosts, that is roughly twenty Sundays of people in the living room, plus a playoff run and a February party. Most buyers tour with a list built around bedrooms, bathrooms and commute. Hosting rarely makes that list, which is how a house that checks out on paper ends up with eight friends in October and four of them standing behind the couch watching the screen sideways.

A game day house is a home whose main gathering room seats everyone facing a single screen, with the kitchen, a bathroom and guest parking reachable without crossing in front of that screen. Square footage is not the measure. Layout is, and it comes down to a short list of specifics that can be checked during a showing.

What should a football fan look for in a home?

A football fan should look for one room with an uninterrupted wall for a screen and seating that all faces it, a kitchen with a clear sightline into that room, a bathroom on the entertaining level, enough outlets and broadband to carry a full house and parking for several guest vehicles. Room count matters less than the capacity of the single best room.

The viewing room

Start with the walls. A hosting room needs one uninterrupted wall wide enough for a large screen, and no window directly opposite it. Afternoon sun facing a screen can ruin a 4:25 p.m. kickoff, and blackout treatments are an expense buyers rarely price in.

Check the room’s proportions next. Long narrow living rooms force half the seating into bad viewing angles. THX recommends a viewing angle of 36 to 40 degrees, which places a seat at roughly 1.2 times the screen’s diagonal measurement. SMPTE sets a 30 degree minimum, which sits closer to 1.6 times the diagonal. The older rule of thumb of 1.5 to 2.5 times the diagonal was built around 1080p sets and runs long for 4K. By any of those standards, a room that seats people at 6 feet and at 20 feet from the same screen will disappoint someone.

Watch for the fireplace problem. Homes that center the living room on a fireplace often leave only one mounting spot, and it sits high enough to strain necks for three hours. Heat and electronics are also a poor combination above an active firebox.

Seating math

Count the seats that can face one screen, not the number of rooms. A house with four living spaces that each seat three is worse for hosting than a house with one room that seats ten.

A large sectional plus a walkway behind it needs real depth. Stand in the room, picture the furniture, then walk the path someone would take to reach the kitchen without crossing in front of the screen. If that path does not exist, every trip for a drink blocks the play.

The kitchen connection

This is the feature fans underestimate most. A closed galley kitchen means whoever is cooking misses the entire second quarter. An island with seating, a wide pass-through or a genuine open sightline from the sink to the screen changes how the day goes.

Look at counter run length for laying out food, refrigerator capacity and whether there is space and an outlet for a second refrigerator in the garage or basement. Beverage volume for a full house is the thing that breaks an otherwise fine kitchen.

Bathroom access

A powder room on the entertaining level is worth more on a Sunday than an extra bedroom. If the only accessible bathroom requires guests to walk down a hallway past bedrooms or up a flight of stairs, that is a daily-use compromise, not just a game day one.

Power, sound and connectivity

Count outlets on the intended media wall. A screen, a soundbar, a streaming device and a console can exhaust a single duplex outlet fast, and older homes may have that wall on a shared circuit with the kitchen.

Confirm broadband providers and available speeds at the specific address rather than the neighborhood. Streaming a game while a full house is on the same network is a real load, and service availability can change from one side of a street to the other.

In townhomes, condos and duplexes, ask about wall construction and sound transfer. A cheering room shares more than a wall with the neighbor’s bedroom.

Overflow space

A finished basement, bonus room or den does two jobs. It absorbs guests who want a second game on a second screen, and it gives younger guests somewhere to be that is not the middle of the main room. Homes with a single gathering space cap the guest list whether the owner intends to or not.

Parking and arrival

Six cars arriving at 12:45 p.m. is a logistics problem. Check driveway width and depth, whether the street allows parking on both sides, whether the neighborhood has permit restrictions and how far guests would walk in November.

Garages deserve a second look here. A garage with a floor drain, a dedicated circuit and enough clearance to open the door and set up chairs becomes a genuine tailgate space in cold weather.

Outdoor space and heat

Covered patios extend the season. Look for an existing gas line for a heater or grill, since adding one later is not a small job. Fire pit rules vary by municipality and some HOAs restrict them entirely, so confirm rather than assume.

Rules and neighbors

Review HOA or condo documents for restrictions on guest parking, noise hours, exterior flags and banners and short-term rentals. Buyers who plan to host regularly should read those sections before waiving contingencies, not after. More on evaluating a home before an offer is in the Home Buyer’s Hub.

What to check during a showing
Bring a tape measure. Measure the media wall and the depth from that wall to the far seating position.
Stand where the couch would go. Look at the wall, then look for windows behind that spot.
Count outlets on the media wall and check the panel for available circuit capacity.
Ask which internet providers serve the address. Sellers or the listing agent can usually confirm.
Tour at game time. A 1:00 p.m. or 4:25 p.m. showing shows exactly how the light hits.
Walk the guest route from the front door to the seating to the bathroom to the kitchen.
Park where guests would park and time the walk to the door.
In attached homes, listen. Stand in the viewing room and note what carries through the shared wall.
Trade-offs a fan should think through

Open concept versus a separate den. Open plans host better and contain sound worse. A household where one person wants the game and another wants quiet may be better served by a dedicated room with a door than by the layout that photographs best.

Basement versus main floor. Basements offer light control and noise isolation. They also mean guests move away from the kitchen and bathroom on the main level, which either works or creates constant stair traffic depending on the floor plan.

Buying near a stadium. Stadium districts often bring transit access, walkable restaurants and steady municipal investment. They also bring game day traffic, permit parking, noise and street closures. Visit on a game day and on an ordinary Tuesday before deciding.

From kickoff to closing

Where a buyer should be at each point in the season.

Kickoff Game	September 9, 2026	Pre-approved, agent selected, must-have list written

Midseason	Late October 2026	Offer accepted, inspection underway
Regular season ends	January 10, 2027	Closed, moved in, furniture placed
Super Bowl LXI	February 14, 2027	Hosting the party in the new house
Selling to the game day buyer this fall

Sellers listing in September and October are showing to people who are picturing exactly the scenario above. A few adjustments speak directly to them, and the Home Seller’s Hub covers the rest of the fall listing prep.

Stage the room around the screen. Removing the television entirely leaves buyers guessing where it goes. Show the arrangement working.
Demonstrate capacity. Stage seating for the number of people the room actually holds rather than a minimalist two-chair vignette.
Put internet speed in the listing remarks. It is a searchable differentiator that most listings omit.
Clear and light the garage. A clean garage with visible outlets reads as usable space.
Photograph the covered patio with the heater or fire feature in use.
Service the furnace and clear the gutters before photos, since fall buyers and inspectors check both first.

Sellers weighing whether fall is the right window can start with a home value estimate.

Write the list before touring

Fans who name three non-negotiables in advance, whether that is a wall without a window across from it, a powder room off the main living space or a garage that fits a second refrigerator, make faster decisions and regret fewer of them. A local REMAX agent can screen listings against that list before anyone spends a Sunday driving.

Frequently asked questions
What should a buyer look for in a home for hosting football games?

Prioritize one room with an uninterrupted wall for a screen and seating that all faces it, a kitchen with a sightline into that room, a bathroom on the entertaining level, adequate outlets and broadband and parking for multiple guest vehicles.

How much space is needed to entertain during football season?

Seating capacity in a single room matters more than total square footage. A room that comfortably seats eight to ten people facing one screen serves a typical game day better than several smaller separate spaces.

How far should seating be from the television?

THX recommends a viewing angle of 36 to 40 degrees, which places a seat at roughly 1.2 times the screen’s diagonal measurement. SMPTE sets a 30 degree minimum, closer to 1.6 times the diagonal. Rooms that force some seats far outside that range create uneven viewing.

Is an open floor plan better for hosting football games?

Open plans keep the kitchen in the sightline and hold larger groups in one space, which suits hosting. The trade-off is sound. Noise carries to the rest of the house, so a household that needs a quiet room during games may prefer a dedicated den with a door.

Is a finished basement good for watching football?

Basements offer strong light control and noise isolation, which suits game watching. The trade-off is distance from the kitchen and main floor bathroom, so the value depends on the specific floor plan.

Should sellers hide the television when staging?

Removing it entirely forces buyers to guess where a screen would go. Staging the room with the television in place and seating arranged around it shows the space working for its most likely use.
